dhpak2.1:3.1: “Heedfulness is the deathless state,” {1.161} this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence
dhpak2.1:3.2: at Ghosita monastery near Kosambī, and it was with reference to the loss by death of the five hundred women led by
dhpak2.1:3.3: Sāmāvatī, and of Māgandiyā and her five hundred kinswomen. From beginning to end the story is as follows: [28.247]
dhpak2.1:4.1: Once upon a time King Allakappa ruled over the kingdom of Allakappa and King Veṭhadīpaka ruled
dhpak2.1:4.2: over the kingdom of Veṭhadīpaka. They had been intimate friends since their boyhood days and had
dhpak2.1:4.3: received their education in the house of the same teacher. On the death of their fathers they
dhpak2.1:4.4: raised the royal parasol and became rulers of kingdoms, each of which was ten leagues in extent.
dhpak2.1:5.1: As they met from time to time, and stood and sat and lay down to sleep together, and watched the multitudes
dhpak2.1:5.2: being born into the world and dying again, they came to the conclusion: “When a man goes to the world
dhpak2.1:5.3: beyond he can take nothing with him; {1.162} he must leave everything behind him when he goes there; even
dhpak2.1:5.4: his own body does not follow him; of what use to us is the life of the householder? Let us go forth.”
dhpak2.1:6.1: Accordingly they resigned their kingdoms to son and wife, went forth in the seers’ going forth, and took up their
dhpak2.1:6.2: residence in the Himālayas. And they took counsel together, saying: “Although we have renounced our kingdoms and went forth,
dhpak2.1:6.3: we shall encounter no difficulty in gaining a living; but if we reside together in the same place, our life will be
dhpak2.1:6.4: quite unlike the life of ascetics; therefore let us live apart. You live on this mountain; I will live on that. Every
dhpak2.1:6.5: fortnight, on the Observance Day, we will meet together.” Then this thought occurred to them: “Under this arrangement
dhpak2.1:6.6: [28.248] neither of us will be in regular communication with the other; but in order that each of us may know whether
dhpak2.1:6.7: the other is living or not, you light a fire on your mountain, and I will light a fire on mine.” And this they did.
dhpak2.1:7.1: After a time the ascetic Veṭhadīpaka died and was reborn as a Lord of Devas of mighty power. A fortnight later
dhpak2.1:7.2: Allakappa saw no fire on the mountain and knew that his comrade was dead. As soon as ever Veṭhadīpaka was reborn, he
dhpak2.1:7.3: surveyed his own heavenly glory, considered the deeds of his former existence, reviewed the austerities he had
dhpak2.1:7.4: performed from the day when he went forth, and said to himself: “I will go see my comrade.” Accordingly he laid aside
dhpak2.1:7.5: his form, disguised himself as a wayfarer, went to Allakappa, worshipped him, and stood respectfully on one side.
dhpak2.1:8.1: Allakappa said to him: “Whence have you come?” {1.163} – “I am a wayfarer, venerable Sir; I have come a long distance.
dhpak2.1:8.2: But, venerable Sir, does your honor reside entirely alone in this place? Is there no one else here?” – “I have
dhpak2.1:8.3: single comrade.” – “Where is he?” – “He resides on that mountain; but as he failed to light a fire on the Observance
dhpak2.1:8.4: Day, I know he must be dead.” – “Is that so, venerable Sir?” – “That is so, friend.” – “I am he, venerable
dhpak2.1:8.5: Sir.” – “Where were you reborn?” – “Venerable Sir, I was reborn in the Deva Realm as a Lord of Devas of mighty power.
dhpak2.1:8.6: I have returned to see your honor. Does your honorable self reside in this place undisturbed, or are you subject
dhpak2.1:8.7: to some annoyance?” – “Yes, friend, I am bothered to death by the elephants.” – “Venerable Sir, what do the elephants
dhpak2.1:8.8: do to trouble you?” – “They drop dung on the ground I have swept clean, and they stamp with their feet and
dhpak2.1:8.9: kick up the dust. What with removing the dung and smoothing the ground, I am all worn out.” – “Well, would you like
dhpak2.1:8.10: to keep them away?” – “Yes, friend.” – “Well then, I will provide you with means whereby you can keep them away.”
dhpak2.1:9.1: Accordingly Veṭhadīpaka gave Allakappa a lute to charm elephants with and likewise taught him spells for charming
dhpak2.1:9.2: elephants. Now as he presented the lute to him, he showed him three strings and taught him three spells.
dhpak2.1:9.3: “Strike this string,” said he, “and utter this spell, and the elephants will turn and run away without so
dhpak2.1:9.4: much as daring even to look at you; strike this string and utter this spell, and they will turn and run away,
dhpak2.1:9.5: eyeing you at every step; strike this string and utter this spell, and the leader of the herd will come up
dhpak2.1:9.6: and offer you his back. Now do as you like.” With these words {1.164} he departed. [28.249] Thereafter the
dhpak2.1:9.7: ascetic lived in peace, driving the elephants away by uttering the proper spell and striking the proper string.
dhpak2.1:10.1: At this time Parantapa was king of Kosambī. One day he was sitting out in the open air basking himself
dhpak2.1:10.2: in the rays of the newly risen sun, and beside him sat his queen, great with child. The queen was wearing
dhpak2.1:10.3: the king’s cloak, a crimson blanket worth 100,000 coins; and as she sat there conversing with the king
dhpak2.1:10.4: she removed from the king’s finger the royal signet, worth 100,000 coins, and slipped it on her own.
dhpak2.1:11.1: Just at that moment a monster bird came soaring through the air. Seeing the queen and mistaking her for a piece of meat,
dhpak2.1:11.2: he spread his wings and swooped down. When the king heard the bird swoop down, he sprang to his feet and entered the
dhpak2.1:11.3: royal palace. But the queen, because she was great with child and because she was of a timid nature, was unable to
dhpak2.1:11.4: make haste. The bird pounced upon her, caught her up in the cage of his talons, and soared away with her into the air.
dhpak2.1:12.1: These birds are said to possess the strength of five elephants; they are therefore able to
dhpak2.1:12.2: convey their victims through the air, settle wherever they wish, and devour their flesh.
dhpak2.1:13.1: As the queen was being carried away by the bird, terrified though she was with the fear of death, she preserved her
dhpak2.1:13.2: presence of mind and thought to herself: “Animals stand in great fear of the human voice. Therefore if I cry
dhpak2.1:13.3: out, this bird will drop me the instant he hears the sound of my voice. But in that case I should accomplish only my
dhpak2.1:13.4: own destruction and that of my unborn child. If, however, I wait until he settles somewhere and begins to eat,
dhpak2.1:13.5: then I can make a noise and frighten him away.” Through her own wisdom, therefore, she kept patience and endured.
dhpak2.1:14.1: Now there stood at that time in the Himālaya country a banyan tree which, although of brief growth,
dhpak2.1:14.2: had attained great size {1.165} and was like a pavilion in form; and to this tree that bird was
dhpak2.1:14.3: accustomed to convey the carcasses of wild animals and eat them. To this very tree, therefore, the
dhpak2.1:14.4: bird conveyed the queen, lodged her in a fork of the tree, and watched the path leading to the tree.
dhpak2.1:15.1: It is the nature of these birds, we are told, to watch the path leading to their tree.
dhpak2.1:15.2: At that moment the queen, thinking to herself: “Now is the time to frighten him away,”
dhpak2.1:15.3: raised both her hands, clapped them together and shouted, and frightened the bird away.
dhpak2.1:16.1: At sunset the pains of travail came upon her, and at the same time [28.250] from all the four quarters of
dhpak2.1:16.2: heaven arose a great storm. The delicate queen, half dead with suffering, with no one beside her to say to her:
dhpak2.1:16.3: “Fear not, lady,” slept not at all throughout the night. As the night grew bright, the clouds scattered,
dhpak2.1:16.4: the dawn came, and her child was born at one and the same moment. Because the child was born at the time
dhpak2.1:16.5: (utu) of a storm, at the time when she was upon a mountain, and at the time of dawn, she named her son Udena.
dhpak2.1:17.1: Not far from that tree was the place of residence of the ascetic Allakappa. Now on rainy days it was the custom
dhpak2.1:17.2: of the ascetic not to go into the forest for fruits and berries, for fear of the cold. Instead he used to go
dhpak2.1:17.3: to the foot of the tree and gather up the bones from which the birds had picked the flesh; then he would pound
dhpak2.1:17.4: the bones, make broth of them, and drink the broth. On that very day, therefore, he went there to get bones. As
dhpak2.1:17.5: he was picking up bones at the foot of the tree, {1.166} he heard the voice of a child in the branches above.
dhpak2.1:18.1: Looking up, he saw the queen. “Who are you?” said he. “I am a woman.” – “How did you get there?” – “A
dhpak2.1:18.2: monster bird brought me here.” – “Come down,” he said. “Your honor, I am afraid to come down on account of a
dhpak2.1:18.3: difference of caste.” – “Of what caste are you?” – “Of the noble caste.” – “I am also of the noble caste.”
dhpak2.1:18.4: – “Well then, give me the password of the noble caste.” He did so. “Well then, climb up and set down my
dhpak2.1:18.5: boy.” Finding a way to climb the tree on one side, he climbed up and took the boy in his arms; obeying
dhpak2.1:18.6: the queen’s behest not to touch her with his hand, he set the boy down; then the queen herself came down.
dhpak2.1:19.1: The ascetic conducted the queen along the path to his hermitage and cared for her tenderly without in
dhpak2.1:19.2: any way violating his vow of chastity. He brought honey free from flies and gave it to her; he brought
dhpak2.1:19.3: rice that grew of itself and prepared broth and gave it to her. Thus did he minister to her needs.
dhpak2.1:20.1: After a time she thought to herself: “For my part I know neither the way to come nor the way to go, nor
dhpak2.1:20.2: can I repose absolute confidence even in this ascetic. Now if he were to leave us and go elsewhere,
dhpak2.1:20.3: we should both perish right here. I must by some means seduce him to violate his vow of chastity, so
dhpak2.1:20.4: that he will not abandon us. Accordingly she displayed herself before him with under and upper garments
dhpak2.1:20.5: in disarray, and thus seduced him to violate his vow of chastity; thenceforth the two lived together.
dhpak2.1:21.1: One day, as the ascetic was observing a conjunction of a constellation with one of the lunar mansions, he saw the
dhpak2.1:21.2: eclipse of [28.251] Parantapa’s star. “My lady,” he said: “Parantapa, king of Kosambī, is dead.” {1.167} – “Noble
dhpak2.1:21.3: sir, why do you speak thus? Why do you bear ill-will against him?” – “I bear him no ill-will, my lady. I say
dhpak2.1:21.4: this because I have just seen the eclipse of his star.” She burst into tears. “Why do you weep?” he asked. Then
dhpak2.1:21.5: she told him that Parantapa was her own husband. The ascetic replied: “Weep not, my lady; whoever is born is
dhpak2.1:21.6: certain to die.” – “I know that, noble sir.” – “Then why do you weep?” – “I weep, noble sir, because it pains me to
dhpak2.1:21.7: think: ‘To my son belongs the sovereignty by right of succession; had he been there, he would have raised the
dhpak2.1:21.8: white parasol; now he has become one of the common herd.’” – “Never mind, my lady; be not disturbed. If you desire
dhpak2.1:21.9: that he shall receive the sovereignty, I will devise some means by which he shall receive it.” Accordingly the
dhpak2.1:21.10: ascetic gave the boy the lute to charm elephants with and likewise taught him the spells for charming elephants.
dhpak2.1:22.1: Now at that time many thousands of elephants came and sat at the foot of the banyan tree. So the ascetic
dhpak2.1:22.2: said to the boy: “Climb the tree before the elephants come, and when they come, utter this spell
dhpak2.1:22.3: and strike this string, and they will all turn and run away, without even so much as daring to look
dhpak2.1:22.4: at you; then descend and come to me.” The boy did as he was told, and then went and told the ascetic.
dhpak2.1:23.1: On the second day the ascetic said to him: “Today utter this spell and strike this string, if you please, and they will
dhpak2.1:23.2: turn and run away, eyeing you at every step.” On that day also the boy did as he was told, and then went {1.168} and
dhpak2.1:23.3: told the ascetic. On the third day the ascetic said to him: “Today utter this spell and strike this string, and the
dhpak2.1:23.4: leader of the herd will come and offer you his back.” The boy did as he was told and reported this also to the ascetic.
dhpak2.1:24.1: Then the ascetic addressed the mother, saying: “My lady, give your son his message and he will go hence and
dhpak2.1:24.2: become king.” So she addressed her son, saying: “You must say: ‘I am the son of King Parantapa of Kosambī; a
dhpak2.1:24.3: monster bird carried my mother off while she was great with child.’ Then you must utter the names of the
dhpak2.1:24.4: commander-in-chief and the other generals. If they still refuse to believe you, you must show them this blanket which
dhpak2.1:24.5: was your father’s cloak and this signet-ring which he wore on his finger.” With these words she dismissed him.
dhpak2.1:25.1: The boy said to the ascetic: “Now what shall I do?” The ascetic replied: “Seat yourself on the lowest branch of the
dhpak2.1:25.2: tree, utter this spell and strike this string, and the leader of the elephants will approach and offer you his back.
dhpak2.1:25.3: Seat yourself on his back, go to your kingdom, and take the sovereignty.” The boy did reverence to his parents,
dhpak2.1:25.4: and following the instructions of the ascetic, seated himself on the back of the elephant and whispered in his ear:
dhpak2.1:25.5: “I am the son of King [28.252] Parantapa of Kosambī. Take me and give me the sovereignty which I have inherited from
dhpak2.1:25.6: my father.” When the elephant heard that, he trumpeted: “Let many thousands of elephants assemble,” and many
dhpak2.1:25.7: thousands of elephants assembled. Again a second time he trumpeted: “Let the old, weak elephants retire,” and the old,
dhpak2.1:25.8: weak elephants retired. The third time he trumpeted: “Let those that are very young retire,” and they also retired.
dhpak2.1:26.1: So the boy went forth, surrounded by many thousands of warrior-elephants, and reaching a village on the frontier,
dhpak2.1:26.2: proclaimed: “I am the son of the king; {1.169} let those who desire worldly prosperity come with me.” Levying
dhpak2.1:26.3: forces as he proceeded, he invested the city and sent the following message to the citizens: “Give me battle or
dhpak2.1:26.4: the kingdom.” The citizens answered: “We will give neither. Our queen was carried off by a monster bird when she
dhpak2.1:26.5: was great with child, and we know not whether she is alive or dead. So long as we hear no news of her, we will
dhpak2.1:26.6: give neither battle nor the kingdom.” At that time, we are told, the kingdom was handed down from father to son.
dhpak2.1:27.1: Thereupon the boy said: “I am her son.” So saying, he uttered the names of the commander-in-chief
dhpak2.1:27.2: and the other generals, and when they still refused to believe him, showed the blanket and
dhpak2.1:27.3: the ring. They recognized the blanket and the ring, opened the gates, and anointed him king.
dhpak2.1:28.1: Once upon a time there was a famine in the kingdom of Allakappa, and a man named Kotūhalaka,
dhpak2.1:28.2: unable to get a living, took his young son Kāpi and his wife Kāḷi, and thinking: “I will
dhpak2.1:28.3: go to Kosambī and get a living there,” set out with provisions for the journey. There are also
dhpak2.1:28.4: those who say that he left his home because the people were dying of snake-wind disease.
dhpak2.1:29.1: As they proceeded on their journey, their provisions gave out, and finally they were so overcome with
dhpak2.1:29.2: hunger that they were not able to carry the boy. Thereupon the husband said to his wife: “Wife,
dhpak2.1:29.3: if we live, we shall have another son. Let us cast this child away and continue our journey alone.”
dhpak2.1:30.1: A mother’s heart is known to be tender, therefore she said: “I could never cast away a living child.”
dhpak2.1:30.2: – “Well, what shall we do?” – “Carry him by turns.” When the mother’s turn came, she would lift the
dhpak2.1:30.3: child like a wreath of flowers, [28.253] clasp him to her breast, {1.170} or carry him on her hip, finally
dhpak2.1:30.4: giving him back to his father. When the father took the child, no matter where he held him he suffered
dhpak2.1:30.5: more intense pain than ever from hunger. Again and again he said to his wife: “Wife, if we live, we
dhpak2.1:30.6: shall have another son. Let us cast this child away.” But this the mother steadfastly refused to do.
dhpak2.1:31.1: Finally the child became so tired from being passed back and forth that he fell asleep in the arms of his father.
dhpak2.1:31.2: When the father observed that he was asleep, allowing the mother to precede him, he went and laid the child
dhpak2.1:31.3: on a couch of leaves under a bush, immediately resuming his journey. The mother turned, looked back, and not
dhpak2.1:31.4: seeing the child, asked: “Husband, where is my son?” – “I laid him down under a certain bush.” – “Husband, do
dhpak2.1:31.5: not kill me. Without my son I cannot live. Bring my son back to me.” And she smote upon her breast and wept. So
dhpak2.1:31.6: the husband retraced his steps, recovered the child, and brought him back to her. The child, however, died on
dhpak2.1:31.7: the road. In consequence of having cast away his child on this one occasion, Kotūhalaka was himself cast away
dhpak2.1:31.8: seven times in a later existence. Let no one regard a wicked deed lightly, saying: “It is only a small matter.”
dhpak2.1:32.1: Continuing their journey, they came to the house of a certain herdsman. On that day, as it happened, one of
dhpak2.1:32.2: the herdsman’s cows had calved, and the herdsman was about to hold the customary festival in honor of the event.
dhpak2.1:32.3: Now a certain Paccekabuddha was accustomed to take his meals in the house of the hersdman. The herdsman,
dhpak2.1:32.4: after providing the Paccekabuddha with food, celebrated the cow-festival with an abundant supply of rice-porridge.
dhpak2.1:32.5: When the herdsman saw the visitors, he asked them: “Whence have you come?” They told him the whole story,
dhpak2.1:32.6: whereupon the tender-hearted youth took pity on them and saw to it that they were given rice-porridge with
dhpak2.1:32.7: a plentiful supply of ghee. The wife said to the husband: “Husband, if only you can live, I can live. For a
dhpak2.1:32.8: long time you have not had sufficient food. Now eat to your heart’s content.” So saying, she set the ghee and
dhpak2.1:32.9: curds before him, eating only a little of the ghee herself. The husband ate heartily; but so intense was the
dhpak2.1:32.10: hunger from which he had suffered during the preceding seven or eight days that he was unable to satisfy it.
dhpak2.1:33.1: When the herdsman had seen to it that they were provided with rice-porridge, {1.171} he began himself to
dhpak2.1:33.2: eat. Now under the herdsman’s stool lay a bitch he had raised, and as the herdsman sat there eating, he
dhpak2.1:33.3: fed her with morsels of rice-porridge. Kotūhalaka watched [28.254] him feed her and thought to himself:
dhpak2.1:33.4: “Fortunate indeed is that bitch to get such food to eat!” Kotūhalaka was unable to digest the rice-porridge
dhpak2.1:33.5: he had eaten, died during the night, and received a new existence in the womb of that very bitch.
dhpak2.1:34.1: His wife performed the funeral ceremonies over his body, and remaining in that very house, worked for
dhpak2.1:34.2: hire. Receiving a pint-pot of rice, she cooked it and placed it in the bowl of the Paccekabuddha, saying:
dhpak2.1:34.3: “May these grains of rice bring a reward to your servant.” And she thought to herself: “It would be
dhpak2.1:34.4: well for me to remain right here. The Paccekabuddha comes here regularly; and whether there be alms or
dhpak2.1:34.5: not, I shall have the privilege of paying obeisance to him each day and of ministering to him. By so
dhpak2.1:34.6: doing I shall obtain peace of mind and earn much merit.” And she remained right there working for hire.
dhpak2.1:35.1: After six or seven months the bitch gave birth to a single pup. The herdsman reserved the milk of one cow for
dhpak2.1:35.2: the pup, and in no long time he grew to be a fine big dog. When the Paccekabuddha ate his meal, he invariably
dhpak2.1:35.3: gave him a portion of his rice; and because of this the dog became deeply attached to the Paccekabuddha.
dhpak2.1:36.1: Now the herdsman was accustomed to go regularly twice each day to wait upon the Paccekabuddha, and the
dhpak2.1:36.2: dog always went with him. On the way was a lair of wild beasts, and the herdsman used to frighten
dhpak2.1:36.3: the wild beasts away by striking bushes and ground with a stick and calling out three times: “Su! Su!”
dhpak2.1:36.4: One day he said to the Paccekabuddha: “Venerable Sir, in case at any time I should be unable to come,
dhpak2.1:36.5: I will send this dog for you. Therefore if I send him, please understand that I wish you to come.”
dhpak2.1:37.1: A few days later the herdsman found it inconvenient to go in person. He therefore sent the dog in his place,
dhpak2.1:37.2: saying: “Dear, go bring the noble one.” At the mere word of the herdsman the dog started off. Where he had
dhpak2.1:37.3: seen his master stop and strike bushes and ground, the dog also stopped and barked three times; and when he
dhpak2.1:37.4: was sure that his barking had frightened away the wild beasts, he went on. {1.172} Early in the morning,
dhpak2.1:37.5: having attended to nature’s needs, he entered the hut of leaves and grass, went to the place where the Paccekabuddha
dhpak2.1:37.6: sat, barked three times by way of announcing his arrival, and then lay down at one side. By this the
dhpak2.1:37.7: Paccekabuddha knew that it was time for him to go, and therefore started out. The dog ran before him, barking
dhpak2.1:37.8: constantly. From time to time the Paccekabuddha tested the dog by taking the wrong path; but every [28.255]
dhpak2.1:37.9: time he did so the dog, by standing across the path and barking, intimated to him to take the other path.
dhpak2.1:38.1: One day the Paccekabuddha took the wrong path, and when the dog tried to stop him, without turning
dhpak2.1:38.2: back, he pushed away the dog with his foot and went on. The dog, perceiving that he did not intend
dhpak2.1:38.3: to turn back, took the hem of his undergarment in his teeth and dragged him along until he brought
dhpak2.1:38.4: him to the right path. Such was the strength of the affection of the dog for the Paccekabuddha.
dhpak2.1:39.1: Later on the Paccekabuddha’s robe wore out. When the herdsman provided him with materials for a new set
dhpak2.1:39.2: of robes, the Paccekabuddha said to him: “Friend, it is difficult for a person all alone to make a
dhpak2.1:39.3: robe. I will go to a convenient place and have it made for me.” – “Make it right here, venerable Sir.” –
dhpak2.1:39.4: “No, friend, I cannot.” – “Well then, venerable Sir, do not take up your residence far from here.” The
dhpak2.1:39.5: dog stood listening to every word they said. The Paccekabuddha said: “Wait a moment, friend.” Thereupon,
dhpak2.1:39.6: leaving the herdsman behind, he flew up into the air and departed in the direction of Gandhamādana.
dhpak2.1:40.1: When the dog saw him flying through the air, {1.173} he began to bark and howl, and he
dhpak2.1:40.2: kept this up until the Paccekabuddha gradually faded from view, whereupon his heart broke.
dhpak2.1:41.1: Animals, they say, are straightforward and not given to deceit; men, however, think one thing
dhpak2.1:41.2: in their heart, but say another with their lips. Therefore the Fortunate One said to a bhikkhu:
dhpak2.1:41.3: “The ways of men are past finding out, but the ways of the beasts are easy to discover.”
dhpak2.1:42.1: So when the dog died, because of his straightforwardness and lack of deceit, he was reborn in the Realm of the
dhpak2.1:42.2: Thirty-Three with a retinue of a thousand Accharās, and there he enjoyed glory and bliss unspeakable. When he but
dhpak2.1:42.3: whispered, his voice carried a distance of sixteen leagues; when he spoke in an ordinary tone, he could be heard all over
dhpak2.1:42.4: the city of the gods, a city ten thousand leagues in extent. For this reason he was named Ghosaka, the Deva son.
dhpak2.1:43.1: Do you ask: “Of what was this the consequence?” It was because he barked and howled for love of the Paccekabuddha.
dhpak2.1:43.2: Remaining in the Realm of the Thirty-Three for no long time, he passed from that state of existence.
dhpak2.1:44.1: Devas pass from the Deva Realm through four causes: exhaustion of life, exhaustion of merit, exhaustion of
dhpak2.1:44.2: food, and anger. He that has earned much merit is reborn in the Deva Realm, remains there during the term
dhpak2.1:44.3: allotted to him, and is then reborn higher and higher. Thus he passes through “exhaustion of life.” He that
dhpak2.1:44.4: has earned little merit [28.256] soon exhausts that merit, just as three or four measures of rice tossed
dhpak2.1:44.5: into a royal storehouse disappear; and he therefore soon dies. Thus he passes through “exhaustion of merit.”
dhpak2.1:44.6: Still a third, while enjoying the pleasures of sense, fails through confusion of memory to partake of food,
dhpak2.1:44.7: and the strength of his body being thereby impaired, dies. Thus he passes through “exhaustion of food.”
dhpak2.1:44.8: A fourth, jealous of the glory of another, {1.174} becomes angry and dies. Thus he passes through “anger.”
dhpak2.1:45.1: Ghosaka, while enjoying the pleasures of sense, became forgetful, passed, through exhaustion of food, from the Realm
dhpak2.1:45.2: of the Thirty-Three, and was conceived in the womb of a courtesan of Kosambī. On the day when the courtesan gave
dhpak2.1:45.3: birth to the child, she asked her slave-woman: “What is it?” – “A son, my lady.” – “Very well, put this boy into an
dhpak2.1:45.4: old winnowing basket and cast him away on the dust-heap.” Thus she caused him to be cast away. Courtesans will
dhpak2.1:45.5: bestow care on a daughter, but not on a son, for it is through a daughter that their line of business is maintained.
dhpak2.1:46.1: Crows and dogs surrounded the child and huddled about him; but in consequence of his
dhpak2.1:46.2: barking and howling for love of the Paccekabuddha, not one dared to approach him.
dhpak2.1:47.1: At that moment a man came out and saw the crows and dogs all huddled together. “What does this
dhpak2.1:47.2: mean?” thought he to himself, going nearer. When he saw the boy, he immediately took a fancy to him,
dhpak2.1:47.3: and saying to himself: “I have gained a son,” he picked the boy up and took him home with him.
dhpak2.1:48.1: Now the rich man of Kosambī happened at that time to go to the royal palace. Seeing the Brahmin chaplain
dhpak2.1:48.2: returning from the royal residence, he asked him: “Teacher, have you observed a conjunction of a
dhpak2.1:48.3: constellation with one of the lunar mansions today?” – “Yes, rich man. What else have we to do?” – “What
dhpak2.1:48.4: will happen to the country?” – “Only this: a boy has been born in this city today who will one day
dhpak2.1:48.5: become the principal rich man.” As the rich man’s wife was at that time great with child, he immediately
dhpak2.1:48.6: sent a messenger to his house, saying: “Go find out whether or not she has given birth to a child.”
dhpak2.1:49.1: He received the answer that she had not yet given birth to a child. Therefore, as soon as he had seen the king, he
dhpak2.1:49.2: went home quickly, summoned a slave-woman named Kāḷī, gave her a thousand pieces of [28.257] money, {1.175} and
dhpak2.1:49.3: said: “Go scour this city, find the boy that was born today, and bring him here to me.” While she was scouring
dhpak2.1:49.4: the city, she came to the house where the child was and asked the mistress of the house: “When was this boy born?”
dhpak2.1:49.5: – “Today.” – “Give him to me,” said she, first offering a penny and gradually increasing the amount until finally,
dhpak2.1:49.6: by offering a thousand coins, she obtained him. Then she took him with her and presented him to the rich man.
dhpak2.1:50.1: The rich man gave him a home in his house, thinking to himself: “If a daughter is born to me, I will marry her
dhpak2.1:50.2: to this boy and make him a rich man; but if a son is born to me, I will kill him.” After a few days his wife
dhpak2.1:50.3: gave birth to a son. Thereupon the rich man thought to himself: “If only this foundling did not exist, my own
dhpak2.1:50.4: son would obtain the post of rich man. I had best kill him immediately.” So he said to Kāḷī: “Carry this child
dhpak2.1:50.5: to the cattle-pen, and when it is time for the cattle to come out, lay him across the doorway, and the cattle
dhpak2.1:50.6: will trample him to death. Observe whether or not they trample him to death, and then come back and tell me.”
dhpak2.1:51.1: She carried the child to the cattle-pen, and as soon as the door was opened, laid him across the doorway.
dhpak2.1:51.2: Now at other times the leader of the herd, the bull, came out last of all; but on this particular day he
dhpak2.1:51.3: came out first, enclosed the boy with his four feet, and stood stock still. Several hundred cows came out
dhpak2.1:51.4: on either side of the bull, rubbing against his flanks as they passed. The herdsman thought to himself:
dhpak2.1:51.5: “Hitherto this bull has always come out last of all, but today he came out first and stood stock still in
dhpak2.1:51.6: the doorway of the pen. What can this mean?” Going near, he saw the boy lying under the bull. Immediately
dhpak2.1:51.7: taking a fancy to him, he said to himself: “I have gained a son,” and picking him up, he carried him home.
dhpak2.1:52.1: Kāḷī went back to the rich man and in answer to his question told him what had happened. Said the rich man: “Go to
dhpak2.1:52.2: the herdsman, give him these thousand coins, and bring the child back to me again.” So she brought the child back
dhpak2.1:52.3: again and gave him to the rich man. {1.176} Then he said to her: “Good Kāḷī, five hundred carts start from this city
dhpak2.1:52.4: at dawn on a trading expedition. Take this child and lay him in the track of the wheels. Either the oxen will trample
dhpak2.1:52.5: him under their feet or the wheels will crush him to death. Observe what happens to him, and then return to me.”
dhpak2.1:53.1: She took the child and laid him down in the track of the wheels. The leader of the caravan came first; but
dhpak2.1:53.2: when his oxen reached the [28.258] place where the child lay, they threw off the yoke. Again and again the leader
dhpak2.1:53.3: replaced the yoke and tried to drive the oxen forwards; but as often as he did so, they threw off the yoke
dhpak2.1:53.4: and refused to move. He was still struggling with them when the sun rose. “Why have the oxen acted thus?”
dhpak2.1:53.5: he thought. He looked at the road and saw the boy. “Oh, what a grievous wrong I have done!” he thought. His
dhpak2.1:53.6: heart was filled with joy at the thought: “I have gained a son,” and picking up the boy, he carried him off.
dhpak2.1:54.1: Kāḷī went back to the rich man and in answer to his question told him what had happened. Said the rich man: “Go
dhpak2.1:54.2: to the caravan-leader, give him a thousand coins, and bring the child back to me again.” When she had so done,
dhpak2.1:54.3: he said to her: “Now carry him to the charnel ground and lay him in the bushes. There he will either be eaten
dhpak2.1:54.4: by dogs or attacked by Amanussa, and he will die. As soon as you know whether or not he is dead, return to me.”
dhpak2.1:55.1: She took the child, laid him in the bushes, and stood at one side. But neither dog nor crow nor Amanussa dared to
dhpak2.1:55.2: approach him. Pray, if he had neither mother nor father nor brother nor other kinsman to protect him, what was it that did
dhpak2.1:55.3: protect him? All that protected him was his howling for love of the Paccekabuddha in his former existence as a dog.
dhpak2.1:56.1: Just then a goatherd passed on one side of the charnel ground, leading several thousand goats to pasture.
dhpak2.1:56.2: A certain she-goat made her way into the bushes eating leaves and grass, and seeing the boy, knelt
dhpak2.1:56.3: down and gave him suck. The goatherd called: “He! He!” but she did not come out. Thereupon he said
dhpak2.1:56.4: to himself: “I will beat her with my stick and bring her out.” So saying, he made his way into the
dhpak2.1:56.5: bushes. {1.177} And there he saw the she-goat on her knees, giving suck to the boy. He immediately took
dhpak2.1:56.6: a fancy to the boy, and saying to himself: “I have gained a son,” picked him up and carried him off.
dhpak2.1:57.1: Kāḷī went back to the rich man and in answer to his question told him what had happened. Said the
dhpak2.1:57.2: rich man: “Go to the goatherd, give him a thousand coins, and bring the child back to me again.”
dhpak2.1:58.1: When she had so done, he said to her: “Good Kāḷī, take this child with you, climb the mountain that is known
dhpak2.1:58.2: as Robbers’ Cliff, and throw him down the precipice. He will strike against the sides of the ravine and be
dhpak2.1:58.3: dashed to pieces when he reaches the bottom. As soon as you know whether or not he is dead, return to me.”
dhpak2.1:59.1: She carried the child to Robbers’ Cliff, and standing at the top of the mountain, threw him down. Now there
dhpak2.1:59.2: grew along the mountain [28.259] near that abyss a dense bamboo thicket, and the top of the mountain was covered
dhpak2.1:59.3: with a thick growth of Rosary Pea shrub. As the boy fell, he dropped into this bamboo thicket as into a
dhpak2.1:59.4: coverlet of goat’s hair. Now that very day the leader of the reed-makers had received a gift of bamboo and
dhpak2.1:59.5: accompanied by his son, he had gone to chop that thicket down. As he began his work, the bamboo shook and the boy
dhpak2.1:59.6: cried out. “That sounds like the voice of a boy,” he thought. Climbing up on one side, he saw the boy. His
dhpak2.1:59.7: heart was filled with joy at the thought: “I have gained a son,” and picking up the boy, he carried him off.
dhpak2.1:60.1: Kāḷī went back to the rich man and in answer to his question told him what had happened. Said the rich man:
dhpak2.1:60.2: “Go to the reed-maker, give him a thousand coins, and bring the child back to me again.” She did so. So
dhpak2.1:60.3: in spite of the rich man’s attempts on his life, the child lived and thrived and grew to manhood. Ghosaka
dhpak2.1:60.4: was his name. He was like a thorn in the eye of the rich man, who could not look him straight in the face.
dhpak2.1:61.1: Thinking of a way to kill him, the rich man went to a friend of his who was a potter and asked him:
dhpak2.1:61.2: “When are you going to fire your bake-house?” – “Tomorrow.” {1.178} – “Well then, take these thousand
dhpak2.1:61.3: coins and do a job for me.” – “What is it, master?” – “I have a single base-born son. I will send
dhpak2.1:61.4: him to you. Take him into an inner room, chop him to pieces with a sharp axe, throw him into a pot,
dhpak2.1:61.5: and bake him in the bake-house. Here are a thousand coins, to seal the bargain, as it were. But in
dhpak2.1:61.6: addition I will reward you suitably later.” – “Very well,” said the potter, consenting to the bargain.
dhpak2.1:62.1: On the following day the rich man summoned Ghosaka and sent him to the potter, saying:
dhpak2.1:62.2: “Yesterday I left an order with the potter to do a certain piece of work for me. Go say to him:
dhpak2.1:62.3: ‘Finish the job my father gave you yesterday.’” – “Very well,” said Ghosaka, and set out.
dhpak2.1:63.1: As Ghosaka was on his way to the potter’s, the rich man’s other son, who was playing marbles with some
dhpak2.1:63.2: boys, saw him. And calling to him, he asked: “Where are you going?” – “I am carrying a message to the
dhpak2.1:63.3: potter for father.” – “Let me go there. These boys have won a big stake from me. You win it back and give
dhpak2.1:63.4: it to me.” – “I am afraid of father.” – “Do not fear, brother; I will carry that message. I have lost
dhpak2.1:63.5: a big stake. You play until I return again, and win the stake back for me.” [28.260] We are told that
dhpak2.1:63.6: Ghosaka was skillful at shooting marbles, and that for this reason his foster-brother was so insistent.
dhpak2.1:64.1: So Ghosaka consented to let his foster-brother go in his place, saying: “Well then, go to the potter and
dhpak2.1:64.2: say to him: ‘Finish the job my father gave you yesterday.’” Thus it happened that the rich man’s own
dhpak2.1:64.3: son carried the message to the potter. The potter killed him according to the letter of the directions
dhpak2.1:64.4: he had received from the rich man and threw his body into the bake-house. Ghosaka played marbles all
dhpak2.1:64.5: day and went home in the evening. {1.179} “You have returned home, son?” queried the rich man. Ghosaka
dhpak2.1:64.6: then told him the reason why he had himself returned home and let his younger brother go to the potter.
dhpak2.1:65.1: “Woe is me!” cried the rich man with a loud voice. He looked as though the blood had been drawn from his
dhpak2.1:65.2: veins. He rushed to the potter, wringing his hands and wailing: “Oh, potter, do not kill me! Do not
dhpak2.1:65.3: kill me!” The potter saw him approaching in this wise and said to him: “Master, make no noise; the job is
dhpak2.1:65.4: done.” Thus was the rich man overwhelmed with sorrow as with a mountain. Thus did he suffer great grief,
dhpak2.1:65.5: even as do all who offend against those that are without offense. Therefore said the Fortunate One:
dhpak2.1:66.1: Dhp 137. Whoever offends with a stick those who are inoffensive and
dhpak2.1:66.2: harmless will quickly fall into one of the following ten states:
dhpak2.1:67.1: Dhp 138. Harsh feelings and loss of his wealth, and the break up of
dhpak2.1:67.2: the body, or even heavy affliction, or surely he will lose his mind.
dhpak2.1:68.1: Dhp 139. There may be danger from the king, or slander that is terrible,
dhpak2.1:68.2: he may suffer from loss of kin, or from the destruction of wealth.
dhpak2.1:69.1: Dhp 140. Also his houses may be consumed by flames and fire, and at the
dhpak2.1:69.2: death of the body that foolish one will arise in the underworld. {1.180}
dhpak2.1:70.1: Now under these circumstances the rich man was unable to look Ghosaka straight in the face. “How can I manage to
dhpak2.1:70.2: kill him?” he thought. Finally he thought of a way. “I will send him to the superintendent of my hundred villages and
dhpak2.1:70.3: order him to kill him,” he said to himself. Accordingly he wrote the following letter to the superintendent: “This
dhpak2.1:70.4: is my base-born son. Kill him and throw him into the cesspool. Let this be done, and I shall know how to reward
dhpak2.1:70.5: my uncle properly.” Then he said to his foster-son: “Dear Ghosaka, there is a superintendent over our hundred
dhpak2.1:70.6: villages. Take this letter and give it to him.” So saying, he fastened the letter to the hem of [28.261] his garment.
dhpak2.1:71.1: Now Ghosaka did not know how to read and write, for ever since he was a boy the rich man had striven, although
dhpak2.1:71.2: without success, to kill him. Why, therefore, should he have taught him to read and write? As Ghosaka
dhpak2.1:71.3: set out with his own death-warrant fastened to the hem of his garment, he said to his father: “Father, I
dhpak2.1:71.4: have no provisions for the journey.” – “You have no need of provisions for the journey. On the way, in such
dhpak2.1:71.5: and such a village, lives a friend of mine who is a rich man. Obtain your breakfast at his house, and
dhpak2.1:71.6: then continue your journey.” – “Very well,” said Ghosaka, and bowing to his father, set out on his journey.
dhpak2.1:72.1: When he arrived at the village, he enquired where the rich man’s house was, went there, and saw the rich man’s wife.
dhpak2.1:72.2: “Whence have you come?” she enquired. “From the city,” he replied. “Whose son are you?” – “I am the son of your friend the
dhpak2.1:72.3: rich man, my lady.” – “Then you are Ghosaka.” – “Yes, my lady.” She had affection as for a son for him at first sight.
dhpak2.1:73.1: Now the rich man had a daughter about fifteen or sixteen years of age, and she was exceedingly beautiful
dhpak2.1:73.2: and fair to look upon. In order to keep her safe and sound, her parents lodged her on the topmost floor of
dhpak2.1:73.3: a seven-storied palace in an apartment of royal splendor, giving her a single slave-girl to run errands.
dhpak2.1:73.4: {1.181} At that moment the rich man’s daughter sent this slave-girl to a shop. The rich man’s wife, seeing
dhpak2.1:73.5: her, asked: “Where are you going?” – “On an errand for your daughter, my lady.” – “Just come here a moment.
dhpak2.1:73.6: Never mind the errand. Spread a seat for my son, bathe his feet, anoint them with oil, and then spread
dhpak2.1:73.7: a couch for him. After you have done this, you may do your errand.” The slave-girl did as she was told.
dhpak2.1:74.1: When she returned, the rich man’s daughter scolded her for her long absence. The slave-girl replied: “Be
dhpak2.1:74.2: not angry with me. The rich man’s son Ghosaka has arrived, and I had to do this and that for him,
dhpak2.1:74.3: besides going on an errand for you, before I returned.” When the rich man’s daughter heard the name “rich
dhpak2.1:74.4: man’s son Ghosaka,” love suffused her body, cleaving her skin and penetrating the marrow of her bones.
dhpak2.1:75.1: For she had been his wife in his former existence as Kotūhalaka and had given a pint-pot of rice to the
dhpak2.1:75.2: Paccekabuddha. And through the power of that deed she had been reborn in the household of the rich
dhpak2.1:75.3: man. No wonder her old passion for him returned and overwhelmed her! Therefore said the Fortunate One:
dhpak2.1:76.1: Through former association, or through a present benefit, in
dhpak2.1:76.2: such a way does love arise, like a lotus in the waters. [28.262]
dhpak2.1:77.1: The rich man’s daughter said to the slave-girl: “Girl, where is he?” – “He is lying asleep on the couch.” – “Has he
dhpak2.1:77.2: anything in his hand?” – “There is a letter fastened to his garment.” – “What can be in this letter?” she thought.
dhpak2.1:77.3: So while Ghosaka was asleep, and her mother and father were otherwise engaged, she came down without attracting
dhpak2.1:77.4: their attention, detached the letter from his garment, took it with her, went into her room, closed the door, opened
dhpak2.1:77.5: the window, and through her knowledge of writing read the letter. “Oh!” she exclaimed, “the fool is going about
dhpak2.1:77.6: with his own death-warrant fastened to his garment. {1.182} Had I not seen it, he would surely have been killed.”
dhpak2.1:78.1: So she tore up this letter and wrote another in the name of the rich man as follows: “This is my son
dhpak2.1:78.2: Ghosaka. Procure presents for him from my hundred villages. Prepare a festival in honor of his marriage with
dhpak2.1:78.3: the daughter of this district rich man. Build him a two-storied house in the center of the village
dhpak2.1:78.4: wherein he resides. Surround his house with a wall and with a guard of men, and so provide him with ample
dhpak2.1:78.5: protection. Then send me a message, saying: ‘I have done thus and so,’ and I shall know how to reward my
dhpak2.1:78.6: uncle properly.” Having written the letter, she folded it up and fastened it to the hem of his garment.
dhpak2.1:79.1: After sleeping all day, Ghosaka arose, ate his meal, and went on his way. Early on the morning of the following
dhpak2.1:79.2: day he arrived at that village and saw the superintendent performing his village duties. When the
dhpak2.1:79.3: superintendent saw him, he asked him: “What is it, dear Ghosaka?” – “My father has sent you a letter.” – “What is
dhpak2.1:79.4: it about, dear Ghosaka? Bring it to me.” He took the letter and read it, and then said with an exclamation
dhpak2.1:79.5: of delight: “See, men, how my master loves me. He has sent me a message, saying: ‘Prepare a festival in
dhpak2.1:79.6: honor of my oldest son.’ Bring wood and other building materials immediately.” Having thus given orders to the
dhpak2.1:79.7: householders, he caused a house of the kind described in the letter to be erected in the center of the
dhpak2.1:79.8: village, had presents brought from the hundred villages, conducted the daughter of the district rich man there,
dhpak2.1:79.9: celebrated the marriage festival, and then sent word to the rich man, saying: “I have done thus and so.”
dhpak2.1:80.1: When the rich man received the message, he said: “What I would do, that I do not; what I would
dhpak2.1:80.2: not do, that I do.” Disappointment over the failure of his latest plan, together with
dhpak2.1:80.3: sorrow over the death of his own son, set him on fire within and produced dysentery. [28.263]
dhpak2.1:81.1: The rich man’s daughter gave orders, saying: “Should anyone come here from the rich man, tell me before you tell the
dhpak2.1:81.2: rich man’s son.” {1.183} The rich man said to himself: “At any rate I will not make this rascally son of mine heir
dhpak2.1:81.3: to my property.” With this thought in mind he said to a certain official: “Uncle, I wish to see my son. Send a
dhpak2.1:81.4: servant and summon my son.” – “Very well,” replied the official, and giving a certain man the letter, sent him away.
dhpak2.1:82.1: When the rich man’s daughter heard that the servant had arrived and was standing at the door, she sent
dhpak2.1:82.2: for him and asked him: “What is it, my man?” – “The rich man is sick and wishes to see his son, and has
dhpak2.1:82.3: therefore sent for him, my lady.” – “My man, is he strong or weak?” – “He is still strong, my lady, and
dhpak2.1:82.4: able to take nourishment.” Without letting the rich man’s son know, she ordered that the man should be
dhpak2.1:82.5: given lodging and expenses and said to him: “You may go when I send you. Remain here for the present.”
dhpak2.1:83.1: Again the rich man addressed the official: “Uncle, did you not send a messenger to my son?” – “I did, master, but the
dhpak2.1:83.2: man who went has not yet returned.” – “Well then, try again and send another.” So the official sent another man, and
dhpak2.1:83.3: the rich man’s daughter treated him just as she had the first. The rich man’s condition grew worse; one chamber-pot
dhpak2.1:83.4: went in and another came out. Again the rich man asked the official: “Uncle, did you not send a messenger to my son?” –
dhpak2.1:83.5: “I did, master, but the man who went has not yet returned.” – “Well then, try again and send another.” So the official
dhpak2.1:83.6: sent another man. When the third messenger arrived, the rich man’s daughter asked him the news. “The rich man is a
dhpak2.1:83.7: very sick man, my lady. He refuses to eat and is confined to his bed. One chamber-pot comes out and another goes in.”
dhpak2.1:84.1: “Now it is time to go,” thought the rich man’s daughter. So she said to the rich man’s son: “I learn that your father is
dhpak2.1:84.2: sick.” – “Wife, what say you?” – “It may be only a slight ailment, husband.” – “What is to be done now?” {1.184} – “Let
dhpak2.1:84.3: us take presents from his hundred villages and go see him.” – “Very well,” he said. Having caused presents to be brought,
dhpak2.1:84.4: he started out, conveying the presents in a cart. Then she said to him: “Your father is very weak. If we take all
dhpak2.1:84.5: these presents, we shall be delayed on the way; send them back.” Having sent all the presents back to their own house, she
dhpak2.1:84.6: said to the rich man’s son: “Husband, please stand at your father’s feet; I will stand beside his pillow.” And as they
dhpak2.1:84.7: entered the house, she gave orders to her own men: “Stand on guard both in the front of the house [28.264] and in the
dhpak2.1:84.8: rear.” And when they had entered, the rich man’s son took his stand at his father’s feet and his wife beside his pillow.
dhpak2.1:85.1: At that moment the rich man was lying on his back and the official was rubbing his feet. The latter said to him:
dhpak2.1:85.2: “Master, your son has arrived.” – “Where is he?” – “Here he is, standing at your feet.” When the rich man saw
dhpak2.1:85.3: his son, he sent for the receiver of his revenues and asked him: “How much wealth is there in my house?” – “Master,
dhpak2.1:85.4: of money alone there are four hundred millions; as for objects for employment and enjoyment, such as villages
dhpak2.1:85.5: and fields and men and animals and wagons and carriages, such and such is the total.” It was the rich man’s
dhpak2.1:85.6: intention to say: “All of this wealth I do not give to my son Ghosaka.” But instead of this he said: “I do give.”
dhpak2.1:86.1: When the rich man’s daughter heard this, she thought to herself: “However, if this man should speak again, he
dhpak2.1:86.2: might say something very different.” Accordingly, pretending to be overcome with grief, she disheveled her hair,
dhpak2.1:86.3: burst into tears, and said: “Dear father, do you really mean this? In spite of these words of yours, which we
dhpak2.1:86.4: hear, we are indeed unfortunate.” So saying, she fell on him, struck the middle of his breast with the crown of
dhpak2.1:86.5: her head, and in order that he might not be able to speak again, rubbed the middle of his breast with the crown
dhpak2.1:86.6: of her head, displaying at the same time signs of profound grief. At that very moment the rich man died. {1.185}
dhpak2.1:87.1: They went and informed King Udena of his death. The king had the funeral ceremonies performed over his body and
dhpak2.1:87.2: asked: “Has he any son or daughter?” – “Your majesty, he has a son named Ghosaka; and, your majesty, he bestowed all
dhpak2.1:87.3: his property on him before he died.” Some time afterwards, the king sent for the rich man’s son. Now that day it
dhpak2.1:87.4: rained, and there were pools of water here and there in the palace court. The rich man’s son set out to see the
dhpak2.1:87.5: king. The king opened his window and watched him as he approached, noticing that as he crossed the palace court he
dhpak2.1:87.6: leaped over the pools of water that stood in the court. When he reached the palace and worshipped the king and
dhpak2.1:87.7: stood before him, the king asked him: “Your name is Ghosaka?” – “Yes, your majesty.” The king comforted him, saying:
dhpak2.1:87.8: “Do not grieve at the thought that your father is dead. I will give you alone your father’s post as rich man.”
dhpak2.1:87.9: Then he dismissed him, saying: “Now, dear Ghosaka, you may go,” and stood and watched him as he left the palace.
dhpak2.1:88.1: Now whereas Ghosaka leaped over the water in approaching the palace, he walked through it on his return. The king
dhpak2.1:88.2: sent orders for [28.265] him to return from where he was and asked him: “Dear Ghosaka, is it a fact that
dhpak2.1:88.3: whereas, in coming to me, you leaped over the water, on your return you walk through it?” – “It is even so, your
dhpak2.1:88.4: majesty. Then I was a boy and was fond of play, but now I have been promised a post of honor by your majesty.
dhpak2.1:88.5: Therefore I must now lay aside my former ways and deport myself with modesty and dignity.” On hearing this, the
dhpak2.1:88.6: king thought to himself: “This is a wise man. I will give him the post immediately.” Accordingly he gave him the
dhpak2.1:88.7: wealth formerly possessed by his father and the post of rich man, together with all the hundred villages. Then
dhpak2.1:88.8: Ghosaka mounted his chariot and drove clockwise round the city. Every place he looked at quaked and trembled.
dhpak2.1:89.1: The rich man’s daughter sat talking with the slave-woman Kāḷī. {1.186} “Mother Kāḷī,” said she, “it was through me
dhpak2.1:89.2: that your son obtained all this worldly glory.” – “How is that, my lady?” – “Why, this youth came to our house
dhpak2.1:89.3: with his own death-warrant fastened to the hem of his garment. I tore up that letter and wrote another, ordering
dhpak2.1:89.4: the celebration of a festival in honor of my marriage to him. In this way did I protect him all that time.” – “My
dhpak2.1:89.5: lady, this is all you know about it. But as a matter of fact, from the time your husband was a little boy, the rich
dhpak2.1:89.6: man constantly sought to kill him, and though his attempts were unsuccessful, a large sum of money was spent
dhpak2.1:89.7: solely for the purpose of accomplishing his death.” – “Kāḷī, the rich man was indeed guilty of abominable crimes!”
dhpak2.1:90.1: Having performed his ceremonial circuit of the city, Ghosaka entered his house. Now when his wife saw him,
dhpak2.1:90.2: she thought to herself: “It was through me that he obtained all this worldly glory,” and laughed. The rich
dhpak2.1:90.3: man’s son asked her: “Why do you laugh?” – “For a certain reason.” – “Tell me the reason.” She refused
dhpak2.1:90.4: to do so. He drew his sword and said: “If you do not tell me, I will cut you in twain.” Then she said: “I
dhpak2.1:90.5: laughed to think that it was through me that you obtained all this worldly glory.” – “If what I possess
dhpak2.1:90.6: was handed over to me by my father, where do you come in?” We are told that during all that time Ghosaka
dhpak2.1:90.7: knew nothing about the designs against his life, and that that was why he refused to believe what she said.
dhpak2.1:91.1: So she told him the whole story, saying: “When your father sent you forth
dhpak2.1:91.2: bearing your own death-warrant, I did this and that and protected you.”
dhpak2.1:92.1: “What you say is not true,” replied Ghosaka, refusing to believe her. “I will ask Mother Kāḷī.” So he asked the
dhpak2.1:92.2: slave-woman: “Kāḷī, [28.266] is what she says true?” – “Yes, my lord. From the time you were a little boy your father
dhpak2.1:92.3: sought constantly to kill you, and although his attempts were unsuccessful, a large sum of money was spent for the
dhpak2.1:92.4: purpose of accomplishing your death. On seven occasions you had a narrow escape from death. Now, coming from the village
dhpak2.1:92.5: of which he was headman, {1.187} you have obtained the post of rich man, together with all the hundred villages.”
dhpak2.1:93.1: When Ghosaka heard this, he thought to himself: “How grave a matter this is! But since I have escaped
dhpak2.1:93.2: from so terrible a death, I must no longer live the life of heedlessness. Henceforth, therefore,
dhpak2.1:93.3: I will live the life of heedfulness.” Accordingly he established alms for the blind and the poor, and
dhpak2.1:93.4: employing his friend the householder as steward of his alms, he dispensed a thousand coins daily.
dhpak2.1:94.1: Now at this time there lived in the city of Bhaddavatī a rich man named Bhaddavatiya, and he was a friend
dhpak2.1:94.2: of the rich man Ghosaka, although Ghosaka had never seen him. For the rich man Ghosaka heard, from
dhpak2.1:94.3: traders who came from the city of Bhaddavatī, of the wealth and age of the rich man Bhaddavatiya, and
dhpak2.1:94.4: desiring to be friends with him, sent him a present. Likewise the rich man Bhaddavatiya heard, from traders
dhpak2.1:94.5: who came from the city of Kosambī, of the wealth and age of the rich man Ghosaka, and desiring to be
dhpak2.1:94.6: friends with him, sent him a present. Thus, although neither had seen the other, they dwelt as friends.
dhpak2.1:95.1: After a time snake-wind disease broke out in the house of the rich man Bhaddavatiya. When this disease breaks
dhpak2.1:95.2: out, the first to die are flies; afterwards, in regular order, insects, mice, domestic fowls, swine,
dhpak2.1:95.3: cattle, slaves both female and male, and last of all the members of the household. Only those that break down
dhpak2.1:95.4: the wall and flee, save their lives. Now at that time the rich man Bhaddavatiya and his wife and daughter
dhpak2.1:95.5: fled in this manner, and intending to seek the rich man Ghosaka, {1.188} set out on the road to Kosambī.
dhpak2.1:95.6: While they were still on their way, their provisions for the journey gave out, and their bodies became
dhpak2.1:95.7: exhausted from exposure to wind and sun, and from hunger and thirst. Reaching Kosambī with difficulty, they
dhpak2.1:95.8: bathed in a pool of water in a pleasant place and then entered a certain rest-house at the gate of the city.
dhpak2.1:96.1: Then the rich man said to his wife: “Wife, those who travel in this [28.267] way are displeasing even to
dhpak2.1:96.2: the mother who bore them. Now I have a friend who, they say, dispenses a thousand coins daily in alms
dhpak2.1:96.3: to the blind, the poor, and other unfortunate persons. We will send our daughter there, have her bring us
dhpak2.1:96.4: food, remain right here for a day or two and refresh our bodies, and then we will go and see my friend.”
dhpak2.1:96.5: – “Very well, husband,” she replied, and they took up their residence right there in the rest-house.
dhpak2.1:97.1: On the following day, when meal-time was announced and the blind, the poor, and other unfortunate persons went to
dhpak2.1:97.2: obtain food, the mother and father sent forth their daughter, saying: “Daughter, go bring us food.” So the daughter
dhpak2.1:97.3: of a wealthy house, pride overcome with misfortune, hid her shame, took a bowl, and went with poor folk to procure
dhpak2.1:97.4: food. “How many portions will you have?” she was asked. “Three,” she replied. So they gave her three portions.
dhpak2.1:98.1: She carried the food back to her parents, and the three sat down to eat together. The mother and daughter
dhpak2.1:98.2: said to the rich man: “Master, misfortune comes even to prominent families. Eat without regarding us and do
dhpak2.1:98.3: not worry.” After a good deal of urging, they prevailed upon him to eat. But after he had eaten, he was unable
dhpak2.1:98.4: to digest his food, and when the sun rose, he died. The mother and daughter wept and wailed and lamented.
dhpak2.1:99.1: On the following day the young girl went the second time to procure food. “How many portions will you
dhpak2.1:99.2: have?” {1.189} – “Two.” She carried the food back to her mother, and after a good deal of urging, prevailed
dhpak2.1:99.3: upon her to eat. The mother yielded to her pleading and consented to eat, but died on that very day.
dhpak2.1:100.1: The young girl, left alone to herself, wept and wailed and lamented over the misfortune that had come
dhpak2.1:100.2: upon her. On the following day, suffering the pangs of hunger keenly, she went weeping in the company
dhpak2.1:100.3: of beggars to procure food. “How many portions will you have, daughter?” – “One,” was her reply.
dhpak2.1:101.1: A householder named Mitta, remembering that she had received food for three days, said to her: “Perish, vile
dhpak2.1:101.2: woman. Today, at last, you have come to know the capacity of your belly.” This daughter of a respectable family,
dhpak2.1:101.3: modest and timid, felt as though she had received a sword-thrust in her bosom, or as though salt water had
dhpak2.1:101.4: been sprinkled on a sore. She immediately replied: “What do you mean, sir?” – “Day before yesterday you took
dhpak2.1:101.5: three portions, yesterday two, today you take but one. Today, then, you know the capacity of your belly.”
dhpak2.1:101.6: – “Sir, do not think that I took these for myself.” – “Why then did you take them?” – “Sir, the day before
dhpak2.1:101.7: yesterday we were [28.268] three, yesterday we were two, today I am left alone.” – “How is that?” he enquired.
dhpak2.1:102.1: She then told him the whole story from the beginning. As he listened to her story, he was unable to
dhpak2.1:102.2: control his tears, but was overcome by the power of the grief that arose within him. Finally he
dhpak2.1:102.3: said to her: “My dear girl, if this is the case, do not worry. Hitherto you have been the daughter
dhpak2.1:102.4: of the rich man Bhaddavatiya, but from this day forth you shall be my very own daughter.” And he
dhpak2.1:102.5: kissed her on the head, conducted her to his own house, and adopted her as his own oldest daughter.
dhpak2.1:103.1: One day she heard loud and piercing screams in the refectory, whereupon she said to her foster-father: “Father, why
dhpak2.1:103.2: do you not keep these people quiet when you dispense alms?” – “It is impossible to do it, dear daughter.” – “Father,
dhpak2.1:103.3: it is quite possible.” – “How would you do it, dear daughter?” – “Father, {1.190} put a fence around the refectory
dhpak2.1:103.4: and hang two gates through which the people may pass in and out, allowing only sufficient space for one person to pass
dhpak2.1:103.5: through at a time. Then direct the people to pass in through one gate and out through the other. If you do this,
dhpak2.1:103.6: they will receive their alms peaceably and quietly.” When the householder had heard her plan he remarked: “A happy
dhpak2.1:103.7: device, dear daughter,” and did as she suggested. Now up to that time her name had been Sāmā, but through her construction
dhpak2.1:103.8: of a fence (vati) she received the name Sāmāvatī. From that time on there was no more tumult in the refectory.
dhpak2.1:104.1: Now the rich man Ghosaka had long been accustomed to hear this noise in the refectory and rather liked to hear
dhpak2.1:104.2: it; for it always made him think: “That is the noise in my refectory.” But after hearing no noise at all for
dhpak2.1:104.3: two or three days, he asked the householder Mitta, who came one day to wait upon him: “Are alms being given
dhpak2.1:104.4: to the blind, the poor, and other unfortunate persons?” – “Yes, sir.” – “How then does it happen that for
dhpak2.1:104.5: two or three days past I have not heard a sound?” – “I have arranged matters so that the people now receive
dhpak2.1:104.6: alms without making any noise.” – “Why didn’t you do so before?” – “I didn’t know how, sir.” – “How did you
dhpak2.1:104.7: happen to find a way just now?” – “My daughter told me how to do it, sir.” – “Have you a daughter whom I have
dhpak2.1:104.8: never seen?” Then the householder told him the whole story of the rich man Bhaddavatiya, beginning with the
dhpak2.1:104.9: outbreak of the snake-wind disease and ending with his adoption of the young girl as his own oldest daughter.
dhpak2.1:105.1: Then said the rich man to him: “If this is the case, why did you [28.269] not tell me? My friend’s
dhpak2.1:105.2: daughter is my own daughter.” So he sent for her and asked her: “Dear girl, are you the daughter of the
dhpak2.1:105.3: rich man?” – “Yes, sir, I am.” – “Well then, do not worry; you are my own daughter.” Then he kissed her
dhpak2.1:105.4: on the head, gave her five hundred women for her retinue, and adopted her as his own oldest daughter.
dhpak2.1:106.1: One day a festival was proclaimed in this city. Now at this festival daughters of respectable families, who do
dhpak2.1:106.2: not ordinarily go out, go on foot with their own retinue {1.191} and bathe in the river. Accordingly on that day
dhpak2.1:106.3: Sāmāvatī also, accompanied by her five hundred women, went right through the palace court to bathe in the river.
dhpak2.1:107.1: King Udena stood at his window and saw her. “Whose are those dancing girls?” he enquired. “Nobody’s dancing
dhpak2.1:107.2: girls, your majesty.” – “Then whose daughters are they?” – “Your majesty, that is the daughter of the rich man
dhpak2.1:107.3: Ghosaka, and her name is Sāmāvatī.” Now the king fell in love with the girl the moment he saw her, and immediately
dhpak2.1:107.4: sent word to the rich man Ghosaka: “Send me the maiden they say is your daughter.” – “I will not send her,
dhpak2.1:107.5: your majesty.” – “Do not act thus. Do as I ask and send her.” – “Your majesty, we householders do not give young
dhpak2.1:107.6: girls, for fear they may be beaten and maltreated and dragged away.” Angered by the rich man’s reply, the king
dhpak2.1:107.7: caused the rich man’s house to be sealed and the rich man and his wife to be seized and turned out of doors.
dhpak2.1:108.1: When Sāmāvatī returned after her bath and found no way of entering the house, she asked: “What does this mean, dear
dhpak2.1:108.2: father?” – “Dear daughter, the king sent for you; and when we refused to give you to him, he caused the house
dhpak2.1:108.3: to be sealed and caused us to be turned out of doors.” – “Dear father, you made a great mistake. When one who is a
dhpak2.1:108.4: king commands, you should not say: ‘We do not give.’ You should rather say: ‘If you will take our daughter with
dhpak2.1:108.5: her retinue, we will give her to you.’” – “Very well, dear daughter. If that is your desire, I will do as you say.”
dhpak2.1:108.6: Accordingly Ghosaka sent a message to that effect to the king, and the king accepted his offer, saying: “Very
dhpak2.1:108.7: well.” Then the king conducted Sāmāvatī with her retinue to the royal palace, conferred the ceremonial sprinkling
dhpak2.1:108.8: on her, and elevated her to the dignity of chief consort. The other women became her ladies-in-waiting. [28.270]
dhpak2.1:109.1: Yet another of Udena’s queen-consorts was Vāsuladattā, {1.192} daughter of Caṇḍa Pajjota (Fierce Splendor), king
dhpak2.1:109.2: of Ujjeni. One day, as Caṇḍa Pajjota was returning from his pleasure-garden, he surveyed his own splendor and
dhpak2.1:109.3: asked: “Is there anyone else possessed of splendor like mine?” – “Splendor such as it is, King Udena of Kosambī
dhpak2.1:109.4: possesses exceeding great splendor.” – “Very well, let us take him captive.” – “It is impossible to capture
dhpak2.1:109.5: him.” – “By employing some means or other, let us capture him all the same.” – “It is impossible, your majesty.”
dhpak2.1:109.6: – “Why?” – “He understands the art of charming elephants. By reciting spells and playing his elephant-charming
dhpak2.1:109.7: lute, he either drives elephants away or captures them at his pleasure. No one possesses so many riding-elephants
dhpak2.1:109.8: as he.” – “I suppose it is impossible for me to capture him.” – “If you are bent on doing it, have a
dhpak2.1:109.9: wooden elephant made and turned loose near him. Let him hear of a good mount, be it elephant or horse, and he will
dhpak2.1:109.10: go a long way for it. When he is close by, you can capture him.” – “A stratagem indeed!” exclaimed the king.
dhpak2.1:110.1: So the king had a mechanical elephant made of wood, wrapped about with strips of cloth and deftly painted, and turned
dhpak2.1:110.2: it loose on the bank of a certain lake near the country of his enemy. Within the belly of the elephant sixty men
dhpak2.1:110.3: walked back and forth; every now and then they loaded their shovels with elephant dung and dumped it out. A certain
dhpak2.1:110.4: woodman saw the elephant, and thinking to himself: “Just the thing for our king!” went and told the king: “Your majesty,
dhpak2.1:110.5: I saw a noble elephant, pure white even as the peak of Kelasa, just the sort of elephant your majesty would like.”
dhpak2.1:111.1: Udena mounted his elephant and set out, taking the woodman along as a guide and accompanied by his retinue. His approach
dhpak2.1:111.2: was {1.193} observed by spies, who went and informed Caṇḍa Pajjota. The latter straightaway dispatched armies on
dhpak2.1:111.3: both flanks of his enemy, allowing the space between them to remain open. Udena, unaware of his enemy’s approach,
dhpak2.1:111.4: continued to pursue the elephant. He recited his spell and played his lute, but all to no purpose. The wooden elephant,
dhpak2.1:111.5: driven with great speed by the men concealed within its belly, made as if it failed to hear the charm and continued
dhpak2.1:111.6: its flight. The king, unable to overtake the elephant, mounted his horse. On and on sped the horse, galloping so rapidly
dhpak2.1:111.7: that by degrees the army of the king was left far behind and the king was quite alone. Then Caṇḍa Pajjota’s [28.271]
dhpak2.1:111.8: men, who were posted on both flanks, captured Udena and turned him over to their king. Udena’s army, perceiving
dhpak2.1:111.9: that their leader had fallen into the hands of the enemy, built a stockade just outside of Ujjenī and remained there.
dhpak2.1:112.1: Caṇḍa Pajjota, having thus captured Udena alive, clapped him into prison behind closed doors and celebrated
dhpak2.1:112.2: for three days. On the third day Udena asked his keepers: “Friends, where’s your king?” – “Carousing, for,
dhpak2.1:112.3: says he: ‘I’ve landed my enemy.’” – “What does your king mean by acting like a woman? He has captured a royal
dhpak2.1:112.4: adversary and surely he ought either to release him or to kill him. He has brought humiliation upon us and
dhpak2.1:112.5: is ‘carousing’– indeed!” The keepers went and reported the incident to the king. The king came and asked: “Is
dhpak2.1:112.6: it true that you said thus and thus?” – “Yes, your majesty.” – “Very well, I will release you. They say you
dhpak2.1:112.7: have such and such a charm; will you give it to me?” – “Certainly I will give it to you; but when you receive
dhpak2.1:112.8: it, will you pay me homage?” – “I pay you homage? I’ll not pay you homage.” – “Then I’ll not give it to
dhpak2.1:112.9: you.” {1.194} – “In that case I will have you executed.” – “Do so; you are lord of my body, not of my mind.”
dhpak2.1:113.1: When the king heard Udena’s defiant answer, he thought to himself: “How in the world can I get the
dhpak2.1:113.2: charm? I have it. I’ll have my daughter learn it from him, and then I’ll learn it from her. It would
dhpak2.1:113.3: never do to let anyone else learn a charm like this.” So he said to Udena: “Will you divulge the charm
dhpak2.1:113.4: to another, if the other will pay you homage?” – “Yes, your majesty.” – “Well then, we have in our
dhpak2.1:113.5: house a hunchbacked woman. She will sit behind a curtain; you remain outside and have her repeat the
dhpak2.1:113.6: charm.” – “Be she hunchback or cripple, I will teach her the charm, provided she will pay me homage.”
dhpak2.1:114.1: Then the king went to his daughter Vāsuladattā and said: “Dear daughter, there is a certain leper who knows a
dhpak2.1:114.2: priceless charm. You sit behind a curtain, and he will remain outside and repeat it to you. You get it from
dhpak2.1:114.3: him, for it would never do to let anyone else learn it, and then I will get it from you.” After this sort,
dhpak2.1:114.4: for fear of their making love, did Caṇḍa Pajjota feign that his daughter was a hunchback and Udena a leper. So
dhpak2.1:114.5: Vāsuladattā seated herself behind a curtain, and Udena remained outside and caused her to repeat the charm.
dhpak2.1:115.1: One day Udena repeated the words of the charm over and over again to Vāsuladattā, but the latter was unable to reproduce
dhpak2.1:115.2: it correctly. Thereupon Udena cried out: “Dunce of a hunchback, your lips are too [28.272] thick and your cheeks too
dhpak2.1:115.3: pudgy! I’ve a mind to beat your face in! Say it this way!” Vāsuladattā replied in anger: “Villain of a leper, {1.195}
dhpak2.1:115.4: what do you mean by those words? Do you call such as I hunchback’?” Udena lifted the fringe of the curtain and asked: “Who
dhpak2.1:115.5: are you?” Said the maiden: “I am Vāsuladattā, daughter of the king.” – “When your father spoke to me, he described you
dhpak2.1:115.6: as a hunchback.” – “When he spoke to me, he made you out to be a leper.” Both said: “He must have said it for fear of
dhpak2.1:115.7: our making love.” Then and there within the curtain they made love, and from that time on there was no learning charms
dhpak2.1:115.8: or getting lessons. The king regularly asked his daughter: “Daughter, are you learning your lessons?” – “Yes, father.”
dhpak2.1:116.1: Now one day Udena said to Vāsuladattā: “My dear, a husband can do that which neither father nor
dhpak2.1:116.2: mother nor brothers nor sisters can do. If you will save my life, I will give you a retinue of
dhpak2.1:116.3: five hundred women and make you my chief consort.” – “If you will carry out your promise without
dhpak2.1:116.4: fail, I will save your life.” – “My dear, I will do so without fail.” – “Very well, husband.”
dhpak2.1:117.1: So she went to her father, saluted him, and stood respectfully on one side. Her father asked her: “Daughter, is your task
dhpak2.1:117.2: completed?” – “Not quite completed, father.” – “What do you require, daughter?” – “We must have at our disposal a door
dhpak2.1:117.3: and a mount, father.” – “Why this request?” – “Father, this is what my teacher says: ‘In order to work the charm, a
dhpak2.1:117.4: certain medicinal herb is necessary, and this must be obtained at night at a time indicated by the stars.’ {1.196} Therefore
dhpak2.1:117.5: whenever we are obliged to go out, whether it be early or late, we must have a door and a mount at our disposal.” –
dhpak2.1:117.6: “Very well,” said the king, giving his consent. They secured permission to use a certain door at any time they pleased.
dhpak2.1:118.1: Now the king was possessed of the five conveyances: a female elephant named Bhaddavatī, which could travel fifty
dhpak2.1:118.2: leagues a day; a slave named Kāka, who could travel sixty leagues a day; two mares, Celakaṇṭhī and Muñjakesī, which
dhpak2.1:118.3: could travel a hundred leagues a day; and an elephant named Nālāgiri, which could travel 2,000 leagues a day.
dhpak2.1:119.1: It seems that before the appearance in the world of the present Buddha, the king had been the servitor of a
dhpak2.1:119.2: certain ruler. Now one [28.273] day as this ruler was returning from his bath outside of the city, a certain
dhpak2.1:119.3: Paccekabuddha who had entered the city to receive alms came out with his bowl clean as it had been washed, having
dhpak2.1:119.4: received not a single morsel of food by reason of the wicked influence of Māra over all the residents of the
dhpak2.1:119.5: city. Indeed when the Paccekabuddha reached the gate of the city, Māra approached him in disguise and asked him:
dhpak2.1:119.6: “Venerable Sir, did you receive anything?” – “But have you made it possible for me to receive anything?” –
dhpak2.1:119.7: “Well then, turn back and go in again. Now I will make it possible for you to receive alms.” – “I will not go
dhpak2.1:119.8: back again.” Had the Paccekabuddha returned, Māra would once more have taken possession of the bodies of all
dhpak2.1:119.9: the residents of the city and would have subjected him to the embarrassment of hand-clapping and rude laughter.
dhpak2.1:120.1: Now when this ruler {1.197} saw the Paccekabuddha returning with his bowl clean as it had been washed, he asked him:
dhpak2.1:120.2: “Venerable Sir, did you receive anything?” – “I have gone my rounds and am coming out, brother.” The ruler thought to
dhpak2.1:120.3: himself: “His reverence does not answer the question I asked him, but tells me something I did not ask about. It must be
dhpak2.1:120.4: that he failed to receive anything.” The ruler looked at his bowl and saw that it was empty. Not knowing whether the
dhpak2.1:120.5: food in his house was ready or not, and therefore, brave though he was, not daring to take his bowl, he said: “Wait a
dhpak2.1:120.6: moment, venerable Sir.” So saying, he went home quickly and asked: “Is our food ready?” Receiving the answer that it was
dhpak2.1:120.7: ready, he said to his servitor: “Friend, there is no one possessed of greater speed than you. Make the greatest possible
dhpak2.1:120.8: speed, and when you reach the noble one, say to him: ‘Give me your bowl,’ and then take his bowl and return to me.”
dhpak2.1:121.1: At the mere word of his master the servitor set out, obtained the bowl, and brought it back. The ruler filled the
dhpak2.1:121.2: bowl with his own food and said: “Convey this to his reverence with all speed. I make over to you the merit of
dhpak2.1:121.3: this action.” The servitor went quickly, gave the bowl to the Paccekabuddha, saluted him with the five limbs, and
dhpak2.1:121.4: said to him: “Venerable Sir, the time is short. I went and returned with the greatest possible speed. As the fruit
dhpak2.1:121.5: of this speed, may I obtain the five conveyances able to travel fifty, sixty, a hundred, and two thousand leagues
dhpak2.1:121.6: a day respectively. As I returned and went, my body was heated by the rays of the sun. As the fruit of this,
dhpak2.1:121.7: in the various places where I shall be reborn, may I possess authority equal to the power of the rays of the sun.
dhpak2.1:121.8: My master has [28.274] made over to me the merit of this alms. In consequence of this {1.198} may I be a partaker
dhpak2.1:121.9: of the Dhamma you have seen.” The Paccekabuddha said: “So be it,” and returned thanks in the following verses:
dhpak2.1:122.1: May you succeed in all that you desire and wish for; may all your
dhpak2.1:122.2: intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
dhpak2.1:123.1: May you succeed quickly in what you desire and wish for; may
dhpak2.1:123.2: all your intentions be fulfilled, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
dhpak2.1:124.1: This was the king’s deed in a previous state of existence.
dhpak2.1:124.2: He was now Caṇḍa Pajjota, and in consequence of
dhpak2.1:124.3: this deed he came to possess these five conveyances.
dhpak2.1:125.1: Now one day the king went out to amuse himself in the garden. “Now’s the time to flee,” thought Udena. So he filled
dhpak2.1:125.2: several big leather sacks with gold and silver coins, placed the sacks on the back of the female elephant, assisted
dhpak2.1:125.3: Vāsuladattā to mount, and away they went. The harem guards saw what was happening and went and told the king. The king sent
dhpak2.1:125.4: out a force in pursuit. “Go quickly,” he said. When Udena perceived that a force had set out in pursuit, he opened a
dhpak2.1:125.5: sack of coins and scattered them along the way. His pursuers stopped to pick up the coins and then hurried along. Then
dhpak2.1:125.6: he opened a sack of gold and scattered it along the way. While his pursuers delayed because of their greed for gold,
dhpak2.1:125.7: {1.199} Udena reached his own stockade built without the city. When his men saw him coming, they surrounded him, and
dhpak2.1:125.8: escorted him back to Kosambī. When he arrived there, he sprinkled Vāsuladattā and raised her to the rank of chief consort.
dhpak2.1:126.1: Still another maiden who gained the dignity of chief consort of the king was Māgandiyā. She, we are told, was the
dhpak2.1:126.2: daughter of the Brahmin Māgandiya, who lived in the Kuru country, her mother also bore the name Māgandiyā and her
dhpak2.1:126.3: father’s younger brother likewise bore the name Māgandiya. She was as beautiful as an Accharā. Now her father
dhpak2.1:126.4: was unable to find a husband who was worthy of her; and although scions of all the great families in the country
dhpak2.1:126.5: asked for her hand, her father sent them all away, reviling them and saying: “You are not worthy of my daughter.”
dhpak2.1:127.1: Now one day, as the Teacher surveyed the world at early dawn, he perceived that the Brahmin Māgandiya and his
dhpak2.1:127.2: wife possessed the supporting conditions for the attainment of the fruition of Non-returning. [28.275] Therefore,
