dhpak2.1:127.3: taking his own bowl and robe, he went to a place just outside of a certain market-town, where the Brahmin
dhpak2.1:127.4: was tending the sacred fire. The Brahmin surveyed the person of the Realised One, beholding in him the
dhpak2.1:127.5: perfection of physical beauty, and thought to himself: “There is no other man in the whole world comparable to
dhpak2.1:127.6: this man. I will give my daughter to this man to cherish and support.” Accordingly he said to the Teacher:
dhpak2.1:127.7: “Ascetic, I have a single daughter, and all this time I have not seen a man worthy of her. But you are suitable
dhpak2.1:127.8: for her, and she is suitable for you. For you {1.200} ought to have a wife, and she ought to have a husband.
dhpak2.1:127.9: I will give her to you. Wait right here until I come back.” The Teacher said not a word, but remained silent.
dhpak2.1:128.1: The Brahmin went home quickly and said to his wife: “Wife! Wife! I saw a man who is worthy of our daughter.
dhpak2.1:128.2: Hurry! Hurry! Dress her in her beautiful garments.” So the Brahmin had his daughter dressed in her beautiful
dhpak2.1:128.3: garments, and taking daughter and wife with him, went to the Teacher. The whole city was agitated. “All this time,”
dhpak2.1:128.4: said the people, “this man has said of every suitor: ‘He is not suitable for my daughter,’ and has refused to
dhpak2.1:128.5: give her to anyone. But it is reported that he has said: ‘Today I saw a man who is suitable for my daughter.’
dhpak2.1:128.6: What manner of man can he be? Let us go see him.” So a great throng of people went out of the city with him.
dhpak2.1:129.1: Now when the Brahmin set out with his daughter, the Teacher, instead of remaining in the place mentioned
dhpak2.1:129.2: by the Brahmin, moved away from that place and took his stand in another place, leaving a footprint.
dhpak2.1:130.1: When the Buddhas establish a footprint, it appears only in a trodden place and not elsewhere,
dhpak2.1:130.2: and only those for whom it is established can see it. Let elephants or other wild animals
dhpak2.1:130.3: tread upon a footprint of the Buddhas to render it invisible, or let a violent storm pour forth
dhpak2.1:130.4: rain upon it, or let the roaring winds beat upon it, yet not one of them can obliterate it.
dhpak2.1:131.1: Now the Brahmin’s wife said to the Brahmin: “Where is this man?” The Brahmin replied: “I said to him:
dhpak2.1:131.2: ‘Remain in this place.’ Where can he possibly have gone?” He looked all about, and seeing his footprint,
dhpak2.1:131.3: said: “Here is his {1.201} footprint.” Now the Brahmin’s wife was familiar with the three Vedas,
dhpak2.1:131.4: including the verses relating to the marks. So she repeated the verses relating to the marks, considering
dhpak2.1:131.5: carefully the marks borne by the footprint before her. Finally she said: “Brahmin, this is no
dhpak2.1:131.6: footprint of one who follows the five lusts.” So saying, she pronounced the following verse: [28.276]
dhpak2.1:132.1: The foot of a lustful man will be on tip-toes, of a hateful man it is severly pressed down, the
dhpak2.1:132.2: foot of the deluded man is dragged along, this is the foot of one who has rolled back the veil.
dhpak2.1:133.1: Then the Brahmin said to her: “Wife, you are always seeing crocodiles in the water-vessel and thieves hiding in the
dhpak2.1:133.2: house. Be still.” – “Brahmin, you may say what you like, but this is no footprint of one who follows the five lusts.”
dhpak2.1:134.1: Just then the Brahmin looked around and saw the Teacher. “There is the man!” he said. Thereupon the Brahmin went
dhpak2.1:134.2: to him and said: “Ascetic, I give you my daughter to cherish and support.” The Teacher, instead of saying: “I
dhpak2.1:134.3: have need of your daughter,” or “I have no need of your daughter,” said to him: “Brahmin, I have something to
dhpak2.1:134.4: say to you.” – “Say it, ascetic,” replied the Brahmin. Thereupon the Teacher told him how Māra had pursued him
dhpak2.1:134.5: from the time of the Great Renunciation to the time of the session under the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, and how,
dhpak2.1:134.6: when Māra seated himself under the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, overcome with sorrow at the thought: “Now this man
dhpak2.1:134.7: has escaped from my power,” Māra’s daughters came to assuage their father’s sorrow and endeavored to seduce
dhpak2.1:134.8: him by appearing before him in the forms of women both young and old. {1.202} “At that time,” said the Teacher:
dhpak2.1:135.1: Having seen Taṇhā and Aratī and Ragā, I had no desire for sexual intercourse. What
dhpak2.1:135.2: is this, so full of urine and exrement? I do not want to touch it even with my foot!
dhpak2.1:136.1: At the conclusion of the verse the Brahmin and his wife were established in the fruition of Non-returning.
dhpak2.1:137.1: As for Māgandiyā, she said to herself: “If this man has no need of me, it is perfectly proper for him to say so,
dhpak2.1:137.2: but he declares me to be full of urine and exrement. Very well! By virtue of the fact that I possess birth,
dhpak2.1:137.3: lineage, social position, wealth, and the charm of youth, I shall obtain a husband who is my equal, and then I shall
dhpak2.1:137.4: know what ought to be done to the ascetic Gotama.” And then and there she conceived hatred towards the Teacher.
dhpak2.1:138.1: Did the Teacher know, or did he not know, that she had conceived hatred towards him? He knew. If he knew, why did he
dhpak2.1:138.2: pronounce the verse? For the sake of the other two. For the Buddhas take no account of hatred directed against them,
dhpak2.1:138.3: but teach the Dhamma solely for the sake of those who are worthy to attain the paths and the fruitions. [28.277]
dhpak2.1:139.1: Her mother and father took her and committed her to the charge of her uncle Culla Māgandiya, and then went forth and
dhpak2.1:139.2: attained Arahatship. Culla Māgandiya thought to himself: {1.203} “My daughter is not suited to be the wife of a low
dhpak2.1:139.3: person, but is suited to be the consort of a king.” Accordingly he adorned her with all the adornments, took her
dhpak2.1:139.4: with him to Kosambī, and presented her to King Udena, saying: “This jewel of a woman is worthy to become a consort of
dhpak2.1:139.5: your majesty.” When the king saw her, he fell deeply in love with her, conferred the ceremonial consecration upon
dhpak2.1:139.6: her, provided her with a retinue of five hundred ladies-in-waiting, and raised her to the dignity of chief consort.
dhpak2.1:140.1: Thus the king had three chief consorts with a retinue of fifteen hundred dancing girls.
dhpak2.1:141.1: Now at this time there were living in Kosambī three rich men, Ghosaka, Kukkuṭa, and Pāvāriya. As the beginning
dhpak2.1:141.2: of the rainy season drew near, these men saw five hundred ascetics who had returned from the Himālaya country
dhpak2.1:141.3: going the round of the city for alms. With joyful hearts they provided them with seats, offered them food,
dhpak2.1:141.4: and obtaining from them a promise to reside with them, they provided them with lodging in their own homes
dhpak2.1:141.5: during the four months of the rains. Then, having obtained from them a promise to return and spend the
dhpak2.1:141.6: following rainy season with them, they let them go. From that time forth, after the ascetics had resided for eight
dhpak2.1:141.7: months in the Himālayas, they kept residence during the four months of the rains with the three rich men.
dhpak2.1:142.1: On a later occasion, as the ascetics were on their way back from the Himālayas, they saw a certain
dhpak2.1:142.2: great banyan tree in a forest retreat and went and sat down at the foot of it. The oldest ascetic thought
dhpak2.1:142.3: to himself: “The Devatā who resides in this tree cannot be insignificant. There must be a Deva-king
dhpak2.1:142.4: of great power here. {1.204} How good it would be if he would give this band of ascetics water to
dhpak2.1:142.5: drink!” Immediately the Deva-king gave them water to drink. Then the ascetic thought of water to
dhpak2.1:142.6: bathe in, and the Deva-king gave that also. Then he thought of food, and the Deva-king gave that also.
dhpak2.1:143.1: Then this thought occurred to the ascetic: “This Deva-king gives [28.278] us every single thing we think
dhpak2.1:143.2: of. I wish we might see him.” Immediately the Deva-king burst out of the trunk of the tree and showed
dhpak2.1:143.3: himself. Thereupon they asked him: “Deva-king, you possess great power. What did you do to get it?” – “Do
dhpak2.1:143.4: not ask me, venerable Sirs.” – “Deva-king, please tell us.” But the Deva-king was exceedingly modest, for
dhpak2.1:143.5: the reason that the work of merit he had performed was a very small one, and therefore he did not wish to
dhpak2.1:143.6: tell. However, after a good deal of urging, he said: “Well then, listen,” and told the following story:
dhpak2.1:144.1: The Tree Devatā, it appears, was once a poor man who sought and obtained work for hire from Anāthapiṇḍika and through
dhpak2.1:144.2: him made a living. Now one Observance Day Anāthapiṇḍika asked on his return from the monastery: “Has anyone told
dhpak2.1:144.3: this laborer that today is the Observance Day?” – “He has not been told, master.” – “Well then, cook him his supper.”
dhpak2.1:144.4: So they cooked him a measure of rice. Now the laborer had worked all day in the forest, and when he returned in
dhpak2.1:144.5: the evening, the rice was prepared and given to him. Hungry though he was, he did not eat it at once. “On other
dhpak2.1:144.6: days,” he thought to himself, “there is a great uproar in this house: ‘Give me rice, give me sauce, give me curry,’
dhpak2.1:144.7: but today all have lain down without making a sound, and they have prepared food for me alone. What can this mean?”
dhpak2.1:145.1: So he asked them: “Have the rest eaten?” – “They have not eaten.” – “Why?” – “In this house people eat no
dhpak2.1:145.2: supper on the Observance Days; {1.205} all keep the fast. The rich man requires all to fast, even infants at
dhpak2.1:145.3: the breast, first causing them to rinse their mouths and to eat the four sweet foods. A lamp of scented oil
dhpak2.1:145.4: is lighted, and all, both young and old, retire to recite the thirty-two parts of the body. But we did not
dhpak2.1:145.5: think it worthwhile to tell you it was the Observance Day, and therefore rice was cooked for you alone. Eat
dhpak2.1:145.6: it.” – “If it is proper for me to begin the fast now, I should like to do so.” – “This is a matter for the
dhpak2.1:145.7: rich man to decide.” – “Well then, ask him.” They went and asked the rich man, and he replied as follows:
dhpak2.1:145.8: “If he begins the fast now and rinses his mouth and takes upon himself the Observance Day precepts, he will
dhpak2.1:145.9: earn half the merit of keeping the Observance Day.” When the laborer heard the answer, he began the fast.
dhpak2.1:146.1: Now the laborer had worked all day long and was hungry, and the result was that the humors of his body became
dhpak2.1:146.2: disordered. He bound a girth about his body, and holding the end of the girth in his hand, [28.279] he rolled over
dhpak2.1:146.3: and over. When the rich man learned of this, he took the four sweet foods and with torches borne before him went to
dhpak2.1:146.4: the laborer and asked: “Friend, what is the matter?” – “Master, the humors of my body are out of order.” – “Well
dhpak2.1:146.5: then, get up and eat this medicinal food.” – “You eat it, master.” – “I am not sick. You eat it.” – “Master, as
dhpak2.1:146.6: for keeping the fast, {1.206} I was not able to keep it all, but let me not be deprived of half.” With these words
dhpak2.1:146.7: the laborer refused to eat. “Do not act thus, friend,” said the rich man. But the laborer steadfastly refused
dhpak2.1:146.8: to eat, and when the sun rose, he died even as a garland of flowers withers, and was reborn in that banyan tree.
dhpak2.1:147.1: Therefore the tree Devatā explained the matter as follows: “The rich man was devoted to the Buddha, devoted
dhpak2.1:147.2: to the Dhamma, devoted to the Saṅgha; and it was through him, and in consequence of the merit I earned by
dhpak2.1:147.3: keeping half of the Observance Day, that I obtained this power.” When the five hundred ascetics heard the name
dhpak2.1:147.4: “Buddha,” they arose and stretched out their hands in an attitude of reverent supplication to the Devatā
dhpak2.1:147.5: and said: “Did you say ‘Buddha’?” Three times they caused the Devatā to answer: “I say ‘Buddha.’” Then they
dhpak2.1:147.6: breathed forth the solemn utterance: “This is an utterance difficult to obtain in this world,” and said in
dhpak2.1:147.7: conclusion: “Devatā, you have permitted us to hear a sound we have not heard for many 100,000 aeons of time.”
dhpak2.1:148.1: Then the pupils addressed their teacher as follows: “Well then, let us go to the Teacher.” – “Friends, we have three
dhpak2.1:148.2: rich men who are generous benefactors of ours. Tomorrow we will receive food in their residence, tell them also what
dhpak2.1:148.3: we have heard, and go. Give your consent, friends.” Thereupon they gave their consent. On the following day the rich
dhpak2.1:148.4: men caused rice-porridge to be prepared and seats to be provided. And knowing that the ascetics would arrive on
dhpak2.1:148.5: that day, they went forth and met them, escorted them to their residence, provided them with seats, and gave them food.
dhpak2.1:148.6: When the ascetics had finished their meal, they said: “Rich men, we are going away.” – “Venerable Sirs, {1.207}
dhpak2.1:148.7: did we not obtain from you a promise to reside with us during the four months of the rains? Where are you going now?”
dhpak2.1:149.1: “In the world the Buddha has appeared, the Dhamma has appeared, the Saṅgha has appeared. We are therefore going to
dhpak2.1:149.2: see the Teacher.” [28.280] – “But is it proper for only you to go to the Teacher?” – “It is not forbidden to others
dhpak2.1:149.3: also, friends.” – “Well then, venerable Sirs, you wait, and we also will go as soon as we have made preparations.”
dhpak2.1:149.4: – “If you wait to make preparations, we shall be delayed. Therefore we will go on ahead, and you may follow after.”
dhpak2.1:150.1: So they went on ahead, and seeing the Sambuddha, praised him, worshipped him, and sat down respectfully
dhpak2.1:150.2: on one side. Then the Teacher taught the Dhamma to them in orderly sequence, and at the conclusion
dhpak2.1:150.3: of his discourse all of them attained Arahatship, together with the analytic knowledges. Thereupon
dhpak2.1:150.4: they asked to be given the going forth. “Come, bhikkhus!” said the Teacher. As soon as he spoke
dhpak2.1:150.5: the word, they became full-fledged bhikkhus, possessed of bowls and robes created by psychic power.
dhpak2.1:151.1: Those three rich men procured the requisites for alms, consisting of garments, coverlets, ghee, honey, molasses,
dhpak2.1:151.2: and so forth, and conveying five hundred cartloads apiece, proceeded to Sāvatthī. On reaching Sāvatthī,
dhpak2.1:151.3: they worshipped the Teacher, listened to a discourse on the Dhamma, and at the conclusion of the discourse were
dhpak2.1:151.4: established in Stream-entry. For a fortnight they resided with the Teacher, bestowing alms, and then invited
dhpak2.1:151.5: the Teacher to come to Kosambī. As the Teacher gave his promise, {1.208} he said: “The Tathāgatas delight in
dhpak2.1:151.6: solitude.” Said the rich men: “Venerable Sir, as soon as we notify you by sending you a message, it will be
dhpak2.1:151.7: proper for you to come.” With these words they returned to Kosambī. The rich man Ghosaka erected Ghosita
dhpak2.1:151.8: monastery, the rich man Kukkuṭa erected Kukkuṭa monastery, and the rich man Pāvāriya erected Pāvāriya monastery.
dhpak2.1:152.1: When the rich men had erected these three monasteries, they sent word to the Teacher to come and visit them. The Teacher,
dhpak2.1:152.2: receiving their message, went there; whereupon they came forth to meet him, escorted him to the monasteries, and
dhpak2.1:152.3: waited upon him by turns. The Teacher resided one day in each monastery and always went to receive alms at the door of
dhpak2.1:152.4: the house of the particular rich man in whose monastery he resided. Now these three rich men had a servitor named Sumana,
dhpak2.1:152.5: and he was a gardener. He said to the rich men: “I have been a servitor of yours for a long time, and I should like
dhpak2.1:152.6: to entertain the Teacher. Let me have the Teacher all to myself for just one day.” – “Well then,” said they, “entertain
dhpak2.1:152.7: him tomorrow.” – “Very well, masters,” he replied, invited the Teacher, and made ready the usual honors. [28.281]
dhpak2.1:153.1: Now at that time King Udena was in the habit of giving Queen Sāmāvatī eight coins every day to buy flowers with.
dhpak2.1:153.2: A maidservant of the queen named Khujjuttarā went regularly every day to the gardener Sumana and procured the
dhpak2.1:153.3: flowers. When she came on that particular day, the gardener said to her: “I have invited the Teacher to be my
dhpak2.1:153.4: guest and shall use my flowers today to honor the Teacher. You just wait, join with me in attendance on the
dhpak2.1:153.5: Buddha, and listen to the Dhamma. Then you may take with you the flowers that remain.” {1.209} – “Very well,” said
dhpak2.1:153.6: she, consenting to remain. Sumana waited upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus presided over by the Buddha and took his
dhpak2.1:153.7: bowl that he might pronounce the words of thanksgiving. The Teacher began to pronounce the words of thanksgiving.
dhpak2.1:153.8: Khujjuttarā listened to the discourse on the Dhamma and became established in the fruition of Stream-entry.
dhpak2.1:154.1: On previous days she had been in the habit of appropriating to her own use four coins and of buying flowers
dhpak2.1:154.2: with the other four; but on that day, spending all eight to buy flowers with, she returned with them.
dhpak2.1:154.3: Sāmāvatī said to her: “My good woman, did the king give us twice as much money today to buy flowers
dhpak2.1:154.4: with?” – “No, my lady.” – “Then why so many flowers?” – “On previous days I kept four coins for myself and
dhpak2.1:154.5: brought you only so many flowers as I could buy for four coins.” – “Why didn’t you take the money today?”
dhpak2.1:154.6: – “Because I heard the Sambuddha’s discourse on the Dhamma and acquired understanding of the Dhamma.”
dhpak2.1:155.1: The queen did not revile her and say: “You wretched slave, give me back the coins you have stolen during all this
dhpak2.1:155.2: time.” Instead she said to her: “My good woman, you have drunk the Deathless. Give me thereof to drink also.”
dhpak2.1:155.3: – “Well then,” replied Khujjuttarā, “order that a bath be prepared for me.” So the queen had her bathed with
dhpak2.1:155.4: sixteen bowls of scented water and presented her with garments of fine cloth. One of these garments she caused
dhpak2.1:155.5: her to put on as an undergarment, the other she caused to be thrown over her shoulder; then she had a seat prepared
dhpak2.1:155.6: for her. Khujjuttarā thereupon sat down, took in her hand a painted fan, and addressing the five hundred
dhpak2.1:155.7: women, taught the Dhamma to them just as the Teacher had taught it. On hearing her discourse, all of them attained
dhpak2.1:155.8: the fruition of Stream-entry. Then all of them worshipped Khujjuttarā {1.210} and said: “Friend, from this day
dhpak2.1:155.9: forth do no wrongful deed, but [28.282] be to us as a mother and a teacher. Go to the Teacher and listen to
dhpak2.1:155.10: every discourse he teaches, and then come back and repeat it to us.” And this she did so faithfully that later on
dhpak2.1:155.11: she came to know the Three Baskets by heart. Indeed the Teacher assigned her preeminence, saying: “Preeminent
dhpak2.1:155.12: among my female lay disciples who are learned in the scriptures and able to expound the Dhamma is Khujjuttarā.”
dhpak2.1:156.1: Now those five hundred women said to her: “Woman, we should like to see the Teacher. Show him to us, that we
dhpak2.1:156.2: may honor him with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.” – “My lady, it is a serious matter to live in a king’s
dhpak2.1:156.3: house. You have obtained access to it, but it is impossible for you to leave it.” – “Woman, do not destroy us.
dhpak2.1:156.4: Let us see the Teacher.” – “Well then, make holes in the walls of your rooms large enough to look through. Then
dhpak2.1:156.5: bring perfumes and garlands, and when the Teacher goes to the door of the house of the three rich men, stand
dhpak2.1:156.6: in your several places and look out and stretch forth your hands and worship him and honor him.” They followed
dhpak2.1:156.7: her directions, and when the Teacher went and returned, they looked out and worshipped him and honored him.
dhpak2.1:157.1: Now one day Māgandiyā came forth from her own mansion and walked along until she came to the place where those women
dhpak2.1:157.2: lived. Seeing a hole in a room, she asked: “What is this?” The women, not knowing of the hatred she had conceived
dhpak2.1:157.3: towards the Teacher, said: {1.211} “The Teacher has come to this city, and we stand here and look at the Teacher
dhpak2.1:157.4: and honor him.” – “So the ascetic Gotama has come to this city!” thought Māgandiyā. “Now I shall know what ought
dhpak2.1:157.5: to be done to him. These women also are his supporters. I shall know what ought to be done to them also.” So she
dhpak2.1:157.6: said to the king: “Great king, Sāmāvatī and her followers are disloyal to you and in but a few days will take your
dhpak2.1:157.7: life.” The king replied: “They will do nothing of the sort,” and refused to believe the charge. Even when the
dhpak2.1:157.8: charge was repeated, he still refused to believe it. When she made the charge the third time and he still refused to
dhpak2.1:157.9: believe, she said to him: “If you do not believe me, great king, go to the place where they reside and judge for
dhpak2.1:157.10: yourself.” The king went there, and seeing the holes in the walls of the rooms, asked: “What does this mean?” When
dhpak2.1:157.11: the matter was explained to him, he did not get angry, said not a word, but had the holes filled up and windows
dhpak2.1:157.12: made with openings [28.283] above in all the rooms. Windows with openings above came in at this time, we are told.
dhpak2.1:158.1: Unable to do anything to them, Māgandiyā thought to herself: “At any rate I will do to the ascetic Gotama what ought
dhpak2.1:158.2: to be done.” So she bribed the citizens and said to them: “When the ascetic Gotama comes into the city and walks
dhpak2.1:158.3: about, instigate slaves to revile him and abuse him and drive him out of the city.” So sectarians who did not believe
dhpak2.1:158.4: in the Three Jewels followed the Teacher about when he entered the city and shouted at him: “You are a thief,
dhpak2.1:158.5: {1.212} a fool, deluded, a camel, an ox, an ass, a denizen of hell, a beast, you have no hope of salvation, a state
dhpak2.1:158.6: of punishment is all that you can look forward to.” Thus they reviled and abused him with the ten terms of abuse.
dhpak2.1:159.1: Venerable Ānanda heard this and said to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, these citizens are reviling and abusing us. Let us
dhpak2.1:159.2: go elsewhere.” – “Where shall we go, Ānanda?” – “To some other city, venerable Sir.” – “If men revile us there, where
dhpak2.1:159.3: shall we go then, Ānanda?” – “To yet another city, venerable Sir.” – “If men revile us there, where shall we go then?”
dhpak2.1:159.4: – “To still another city, venerable Sir.” – “Ānanda, one should not speak thus. Where a difficulty arises, right there
dhpak2.1:159.5: it should be settled. Only under those circumstances is it permissible to go elsewhere. But who are reviling you,
dhpak2.1:159.6: Ānanda?” – “Venerable Sir, everyone is reviling us, slaves and all.” – “Ānanda, I am like an elephant that has entered
dhpak2.1:159.7: the fray. Even as it is the duty of an elephant that has entered the fray to withstand the arrows which come from the
dhpak2.1:159.8: four quarters, precisely so it is my duty to endure with patience the words spoken by many wicked men.” So saying, he
dhpak2.1:159.9: taught the Dhamma with reference to himself by pronouncing the following three verses in the Chapter about the Elephant:
dhpak2.1:160.1: Dhp 320. Like an elephant in battle endures an arrow shot from bow,
dhpak2.1:160.2: so will I endure abuse, for many people are unvirtuous. {1.213}
dhpak2.1:161.1: Dhp 321. They lead one trained into a crowd, a king mounts one who has been
dhpak2.1:161.2: trained, amongst humans one trained is best, the one who can endure abuse.
dhpak2.1:162.1: Dhp 322. Noble are the well-trained mules, the well-bred horses from Sindh, and the great
dhpak2.1:162.2: tusker elephants, and even more noble than that is the one who has trained himself.
dhpak2.1:163.1: This discourse benefited the assembled multitude. When the Teacher had thus taught the Dhamma, he said:
dhpak2.1:163.2: “Ānanda, be not disturbed. These men will revile you for only seven days, and on the [28.284] eighth
dhpak2.1:163.3: day they will become silent. A difficulty encountered by the Buddhas lasts no longer than seven days.”
dhpak2.1:164.1: When Māgandiyā had failed in her attempt to drive the Teacher out of the city by abusing him, she thought to herself:
dhpak2.1:164.2: “Pray what can I do now?” Then the thought occurred to her: “These women are his supporters. I will destroy them.”
dhpak2.1:164.3: Accordingly one day, while King Udena was drinking strong drink and she was waiting upon him, she sent the following message
dhpak2.1:164.4: to her uncle: “Let my uncle come with eight dead cocks and eight live cocks. Having arrived, let him stand at the
dhpak2.1:164.5: top of the stairs and announce his arrival. When he hears the word ‘Enter’, let him not enter, but send in first the
dhpak2.1:164.6: eight live cocks and afterwards the others.” And she gave a bribe to the page, saying: “Be sure to carry out my orders.”
dhpak2.1:165.1: Māgandiya came and announced himself to the king. When, however, he heard the word ‘Enter’, he said: “I will not enter
dhpak2.1:165.2: the king’s drinking-place.” {1.214} Māgandiyā then sent her page, saying: “Boy, go to my uncle.” He went, took the
dhpak2.1:165.3: eight live cocks which Māgandiyā’s uncle gave him, carried them to the king, and said: “Your majesty, the Brahmin
dhpak2.1:165.4: chaplain has sent you a present.” – “A most excellent and dainty morsel!” said the king. “Now who will cook them?”
dhpak2.1:165.5: Māgandiyā said: “Great king, the five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī have nothing to do. Send the cocks to them. Let them
dhpak2.1:165.6: cook them and carry them to you.” Accordingly the king sent them, saying to the page: “Go and give these cocks to
dhpak2.1:165.7: these women. Tell them not to entrust them to the hands of anyone else, but to kill them and cook them themselves.”
dhpak2.1:165.8: – “Very well, your majesty,” replied the page, and went and delivered the message. But the women refused to do the
dhpak2.1:165.9: king’s bidding, saying: “We do not take the life of any living creature.” The page returned and so informed the king.
dhpak2.1:166.1: Māgandiyā said: “You see, great king? Now you shall find out whether or not they really take the life of living
dhpak2.1:166.2: creatures. Your majesty, send word to them: ‘Cook them and send them to the ascetic Gotama.’” So the king sent this message
dhpak2.1:166.3: to them. But the page, while pretending to carry the live cocks to the women, in reality went and gave those cocks
dhpak2.1:166.4: to the Brahmin chaplain and carried the eight dead cocks to the women, saying: “Cook these cocks and send them to
dhpak2.1:166.5: the Teacher.” – “This, to be sure, is our duty,” said the women in reply, and going to meet him, they received the
dhpak2.1:166.6: cocks. When the page returned to the king and the latter asked him: “What was the result, boy?” he gave the king the
dhpak2.1:166.7: following report: “The moment I [28.285] said to them: ‘Cook these cocks and send them to the hermit Gotama,’ they
dhpak2.1:166.8: came to meet me and accepted them.” – “See, great king,” said Māgandiyā, “they will not do it for the likes of you.
dhpak2.1:166.9: But you would not believe me when I said to you: ‘Their inclination is towards another.’” But even when the king heard
dhpak2.1:166.10: this, {1.215} he tolerated their conduct and remained silent. Māgandiyā thought to herself: “What shall I do now?”
dhpak2.1:167.1: Now at this time the king was accustomed to divide his time equally among his three consorts, Sāmāvatī, Vāsuladattā,
dhpak2.1:167.2: and Māgandiyā, spending seven days by turns in the apartment of each. Māgandiyā, knowing that he would go on the morrow
dhpak2.1:167.3: or on the day after to the apartment of Sāmāvatī, sent word to her uncle: “Send me a snake, first washing its fangs
dhpak2.1:167.4: with a poisonous drug.” He did as she told him to and sent her a snake. Now wherever the king went, he was accustomed
dhpak2.1:167.5: to take with him his lute for charming elephants, and in the shell of this lute was a hole. Māgandiyā inserted the snake
dhpak2.1:167.6: in the hole and stopped the hole with a bunch of flowers; for two or three days the snake remained within the lute.
dhpak2.1:168.1: On the day when the king was to go to Sāmāvatī’s apartment, Māgandiyā asked him: “To whose apartment
dhpak2.1:168.2: will you go today, your majesty?” – “To Sāmāvatī’s apartment.” Said Māgandiyā: “Your majesty, today
dhpak2.1:168.3: I had a bad dream; you must not go there.” – “I am going all the same.” Three times she tried to
dhpak2.1:168.4: dissuade him from going and failed. Finally she said: “In that case I will go too.” In spite of the
dhpak2.1:168.5: king’s protests she went with him, saying: “Your majesty, I do not know what will happen to you.”
dhpak2.1:169.1: The king, wearing garments, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments given him by Sāmāvatī and her followers, ate heartily,
dhpak2.1:169.2: and then placed his lute by his pillow and lay down on the bed. Māgandiyā, pretending to be merely walking back
dhpak2.1:169.3: and forth, removed the bunch of flowers from the opening in the lute; whereupon the snake, which had been without
dhpak2.1:169.4: food for two or three days, glided from the opening, hissed, raised his hood, and coiled himself up on the top of
dhpak2.1:169.5: the bed. {1.216} When Māgandiyā saw the snake, she screamed with a loud voice: “Oh, your majesty, there is a snake!”
dhpak2.1:169.6: And she straightaway abused the king, saying: “This stupid, unlucky king will not listen to anything I say to
dhpak2.1:169.7: him. As for these shameless scoundrels, what do they not receive from the king? You will live happily just as soon
dhpak2.1:169.8: as the king is dead, but so long as he lives, you will have a hard time. Your majesty, when I cried out to you:
dhpak2.1:169.9: ‘Today I had a bad dream; you [28.286] must not go to Sāmāvatī’s apartment’ you would not listen to what I said.”
dhpak2.1:170.1: When the king saw the snake, he was terrified with the fear of death, the fire of anger was kindled within him, and
dhpak2.1:170.2: he said: “So this is the sort of thing they are capable of doing! What criminals they are! Yet I would not believe
dhpak2.1:170.3: Māgandiyā when she told me of their wicked nature. First they made holes in the walls of their own rooms and sat
dhpak2.1:170.4: there; again, when I sent the cocks to them, they sent them back; today they have let a snake loose in my bed.”
dhpak2.1:171.1: Sāmāvatī delivered the following admonition to her five hundred women: “Friends, we have no other refuge.
dhpak2.1:171.2: Cherish precisely the same feelings towards the king and the queen as you do towards yourselves. Be not angry with
dhpak2.1:171.3: anyone.” The king took his horn-bow, which required a thousand men to string, twanged the bowstring, fitted
dhpak2.1:171.4: a poisoned arrow to the string, and placing Sāmāvatī in front {1.217} and all the other women in a single
dhpak2.1:171.5: file behind her, shot an arrow at Sāmāvatī’s breast. But through the supernatural power of her loving-kindness
dhpak2.1:171.6: the arrow turned back, and returning by the same path it had come, penetrated, as it were, the king’s heart.
dhpak2.1:172.1: The king thought to himself: “The arrow I shot is capable of piercing even a rock, and there was nothing in the air
dhpak2.1:172.2: to make it turn back. But it turned and came back by the same path it went. Indeed this senseless, lifeless arrow
dhpak2.1:172.3: knows her goodness, but I, who am a human being, know it not.” And throwing the bow away and stretching forth his
dhpak2.1:172.4: hands in an attitude of reverent supplication, he knelt before Sāmāvatī’s feet and pronounced the following verse:
dhpak2.1:173.1: I am bewildered, befuddled, all the quarters bewilder me, Sāmāvatī, please protect me, you must be a refuge to me.
dhpak2.1:174.1: Sāmāvatī, hearing his words, instead of saying: “Very well, your majesty, seek refuge in
dhpak2.1:174.2: me,” said: “Great king, in whom I have sought refuge, in him do you also seek refuge.”
dhpak2.1:175.1: Having thus spoken, Sāmāvatī, disciple of the Sambuddha, said:
dhpak2.1:176.1: Do not go for refuge to me, to whom I have gone for refuge, he is the Buddha, O Great King,
dhpak2.1:176.2: he is the Buddha unsurpassed, go for refuge to the Buddha, and be a refuge unto me! {1.218}
dhpak2.1:177.1: The king said: “Now I am the more afraid,” and pronounced the following verse: [28.287]
dhpak2.1:178.1: This is even more befuddling, all the quarters bewilder me, Sāmāvatī, please protect me, you must be a refuge to me.
dhpak2.1:179.1: But she refused him precisely as before. Finally he said: “Well then, I seek refuge in you
dhpak2.1:179.2: and in the Teacher, and I grant you a boon.” – “I accept the boon, great king,” she replied.
dhpak2.1:180.1: The king approached the Teacher, sought refuge in him, invited him to accept his hospitality, and for
dhpak2.1:180.2: seven days gave generous alms. Then, addressing Sāmāvatī, he said: “Rise and take your choice.” Sāmāvatī
dhpak2.1:180.3: replied: “Great king, I have no need of gold and silver, but grant me this boon. Arrange matters so
dhpak2.1:180.4: that the Teacher may come here regularly with his five hundred bhikkhus, so that I may hear the Dhamma.”
dhpak2.1:181.1: So the king worshipped the Teacher and said: “Venerable Sir, come here regularly with your five hundred
dhpak2.1:181.2: bhikkhus. Sāmāvatī and her attendants say they wish to hear the Dhamma.” The Teacher replied: “Great king,
dhpak2.1:181.3: the Buddhas may not always go to one place; many desire their presence.” – “Well then, direct one bhikkhu
dhpak2.1:181.4: to come.” The Teacher directed the Elder Ānanda to go. So Ānanda went every day to the royal palace with
dhpak2.1:181.5: five hundred bhikkhus, and those women every day provided the elder with food and listened to the Dhamma.
dhpak2.1:182.1: One day, after they had listened to the elder’s discourse on the Dhamma, their hearts were filled with joy, and they
dhpak2.1:182.2: rendered honor to the elder by presenting him with five hundred upper robes, {1.219} each worth five hundred coins.
dhpak2.1:182.3: When the king saw that they had not a single garment left, he asked them: “Where are your upper robes?” – “We gave
dhpak2.1:182.4: them to the reverend elder.” – “Did he take them all?” – “Yes, he took them all.” The king approached the elder,
dhpak2.1:182.5: worshipped him, questioned him about the gift of the robes by the women, and learning that the women had given the robes
dhpak2.1:182.6: and that the elder had received them, asked: “Venerable Sir, there were a great many robes, were there not? What
dhpak2.1:182.7: will you do with so many?” – “I shall keep as many as we require for ourselves and send the rest to those whose robes
dhpak2.1:182.8: are worn out, great king.” – “What will they do with their own worn-out robes?” – “They will give them to those whose
dhpak2.1:182.9: robes are in a still worse state of repair.” – “What will they do with their own worn-out robes?” – “They will
dhpak2.1:182.10: make bedspreads of them.” – “What will they do with the old bedspreads?” – “They will make carpets of them.” – “What
dhpak2.1:182.11: will they do with the old carpets?” – “They will make foot-towels of them.” – “What will they do with the old foot-towels?”
dhpak2.1:182.12: – “They will cut them into small pieces, mix them with mortar, and use them to plaster walls with.” [28.288]
dhpak2.1:183.1: “Venerable Sir, although all these are given to your reverences, nothing is lost.” – “Quite so, great king.”
dhpak2.1:183.2: The king was so pleased that he caused five hundred more robes to be brought and placed at the elder’s feet.
dhpak2.1:184.1: We are told that robes worth five hundred coins {1.220} were laid at the elder’s feet in lots of five hundred on
dhpak2.1:184.2: five hundred occasions; robes worth a thousand coins in lots of a thousand on a thousand occasions; and robes worth
dhpak2.1:184.3: 100,000 coins in lots of 100,000 on 100,000 occasions. It is impossible to enumerate the number of robes he received
dhpak2.1:184.4: by ones and twos and threes and fours and fives and tens. We are told that, upon the death of the Teacher, the
dhpak2.1:184.5: elder traveled all over Jambudīpa, presenting to the bhikkhus in all of the monasteries bowls and robes of his own.
dhpak2.1:185.1: Māgandiyā thought to herself: “Whatever I do turns out otherwise than I expect. What shall I do now?” Finally
dhpak2.1:185.2: she decided on a plan. On her way to the garden to amuse herself, she sent the following message to
dhpak2.1:185.3: her uncle: “Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, open the linen-closets and the oil-closets, soak pieces of cloth in
dhpak2.1:185.4: the jars of oil, and wrap these cloths about the pillars. Then assemble all the women within the house,
dhpak2.1:185.5: close the door, bar it from without, set fire to the house with torches, and then descend and go your way.”
dhpak2.1:186.1: Māgandiya went up into the palace, {1.221} opened the closets, soaked garments in the oil-jars, and was
dhpak2.1:186.2: just beginning to wrap them about the pillars when the women led by Sāmāvatī came up to him and said: “Why
dhpak2.1:186.3: are you doing this, uncle?” – “My ladies, the king desires these pillars to be strengthened, and has
dhpak2.1:186.4: therefore given orders that they be wrapped in cloths soaked in oil. It is hard to understand why certain things
dhpak2.1:186.5: should be done in a king’s house and certain other things should not be done. I beg of you, my ladies,
dhpak2.1:186.6: not to remain here with me.” As soon as they had departed and entered their rooms at his suggestion, he
dhpak2.1:186.7: closed the doors, barred them from without, set fire to first one cloth and then another, and descended.
dhpak2.1:187.1: Sāmāvatī delivered the following admonition to her followers: “It [28.289] would not be an easy matter, even with
dhpak2.1:187.2: the knowledge of a Buddha, to determine exactly the number of times our bodies have thus been burned with fire as
dhpak2.1:187.3: we have passed from birth to rebirth in the round of existences which has no conceivable beginning. Therefore be
dhpak2.1:187.4: heedful.” As the fire consumed the house, the women applied themselves to meditation on the feelings, with the result
dhpak2.1:187.5: that some of them attained the fruition of Once-returning, while others attained the fruition of Non-returning.
dhpak2.1:189.1: Now a large number of bhikkhus, returning from their almsround after breakfast, drew near to where the Fortunate
dhpak2.1:189.2: One was, and having drawn near, worshipped the Fortunate One and sat down reverently on one side. And as they sat
dhpak2.1:189.3: there on one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Fortunate One: “Here, venerable Sir, while King Udena was in
dhpak2.1:189.4: his pleasure-garden, the quarters of his women were consumed with fire, and five hundred women led by Sāmāvatī lost
dhpak2.1:189.5: their lives. Venerable Sir, what will be the end, what will be the future state of these female lay disciples?”
dhpak2.1:190.1: “Bhikkhus, some of these female lay disciples {1.222} obtained Stream-entry, others obtained Once-returning,
dhpak2.1:190.2: others obtained Non-returning. Bhikkhus, none of those female lay disciples died without spiritual fruit.” And the
dhpak2.1:190.3: Fortunate One, clearly understanding the matter, breathed forth at that time the following exalted utterance:
dhpak2.1:191.1: The world, bonded to delusion, is seen as being beautiful, the fool, in bondage to cleaving,
dhpak2.1:191.2: is surrounded by darkness. it seems like it is eternal, for one who sees, there is nothing.
dhpak2.1:192.1: So saying, he taught the Dhamma, saying: “Bhikkhus, as living beings pass through the round
dhpak2.1:192.2: of existences, they are not always heedful, and sometimes they commit wrong. Therefore
dhpak2.1:192.3: as they pass through the round of existences, they experience both pleasure and pain.”
dhpak2.1:193.1: When the king heard the cry: “Sāmāvatī’s house is on fire!” he went there quickly, but the house was burned before
dhpak2.1:193.2: he could reach it. While extinguishing the flames, he sat down surrounded by his retinue of courtiers, overwhelmed
dhpak2.1:193.3: with profound grief, and recalled to his mind the virtues of Sāmāvatī. “Who could have done this deed?” he thought.
dhpak2.1:193.4: Coming to the conclusion that Māgandiyā was the author of the crime, he thought to himself: “If I frighten her
dhpak2.1:193.5: by my questions, she will not tell me. Therefore I will employ craft and question her gently.” {1.223} [28.290]
dhpak2.1:194.1: Accordingly he said to his ministers: “Well, until this moment, no matter what I was engaged in or occupied with, I was
dhpak2.1:194.2: apprehensive and suspicious; Sāmāvatī was ever seeking occasion to slay me. But now my mind will rest in peace, and I
dhpak2.1:194.3: shall be able to lie down to sleep in security.” – “Who was it that did this deed, your majesty?” – “Someone who really
dhpak2.1:194.4: loved me must have done it.” Now Māgandiyā happened to be standing near, and when she heard the king say this, she said:
dhpak2.1:194.5: “None other than I could have done this. I alone did it. I sent word to my uncle and ordered him to do it.” – “Except you,
dhpak2.1:194.6: there is not a living being who really loves me. I am delighted. I grant you a boon. Send for all of your relatives.”
dhpak2.1:195.1: So Māgandiyā sent the following message to her relatives: “The king is pleased with me and has granted me a
dhpak2.1:195.2: boon. Come immediately.” The king rendered high honor to all those who came, insomuch that even persons who were
dhpak2.1:195.3: in no way related to Māgandiyā, hearing about it, gave bribes and came and said: “We are relatives of Māgandiyā.”
dhpak2.1:195.4: When the king had them all in his hands, he caused pits to be dug waist-deep in the palace-court, set them
dhpak2.1:195.5: therein, filled up the pits with earth, spread straw on top, and set the straw on fire. When the skin had
dhpak2.1:195.6: been burned to a crisp, he caused the bodies to be plowed with an iron plow {1.224} and to be broken up into
dhpak2.1:195.7: pieces and fragments. As for Māgandiyā, he had pieces of solid flesh ripped from various parts of her body with a
dhpak2.1:195.8: sharp knife, and setting a vessel of oil on the brazier, he had them fried like cakes and made her eat them.
dhpak2.1:196.1: In the Dhamma Hall the bhikkhus began to discuss matters, saying: “It is not right that a female lay
dhpak2.1:196.2: disciple endowed with such faith should suffer such a death.” The Teacher came in and asked them: “Bhikkhus,
dhpak2.1:196.3: what is it you are sitting here now talking about?” When they told him, he said: “Bhikkhus, if you
dhpak2.1:196.4: regard this existence alone, it is indeed highly improper and unjust that the five hundred women led by
dhpak2.1:196.5: Sāmāvatī should suffer such a death. What they received, however, was in every way proper, considering
dhpak2.1:196.6: the wrong they committed in a previous existence.” – “Venerable Sir, what was the wrong they committed
dhpak2.1:196.7: in a previous existence? Pray tell us.” Responding to their request, the Teacher related the following
dhpak2.1:197.1: Once upon a time, when Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, there were eight Paccekabuddhas who regularly
dhpak2.1:197.2: took their meals in the [28.291] royal palace, and there were five hundred women who waited upon
dhpak2.1:197.3: them. Seven of these Paccekabuddhas gone forth to the Himālaya, and the Paccekabuddha who remained
dhpak2.1:197.4: sat down on the bank of the river where there was a tangle of grass, and entered into absorption.
dhpak2.1:198.1: Now one day, after the Paccekabuddhas had departed, the king took those women {1.225} and went to sport in the water.
dhpak2.1:198.2: When those women, who had sported there in the water all day, came out, they were stung with cold. Desiring to warm
dhpak2.1:198.3: themselves, they said to each other: “Seek out some place where we can build a fire.” As they walked back and forth,
dhpak2.1:198.4: they saw the tangle of grass, and thinking it was no more than a heap of grass, they gathered round it and set it
dhpak2.1:198.5: on fire. When the grass burned down and they saw the Paccekabuddha, they cried out: “We are lost! We are lost! The
dhpak2.1:198.6: king’s Paccekabuddha is burning up. If the king finds it out, he will kill everyone of us. Let us burn him well while
dhpak2.1:198.7: we are about it.” So all those women brought firewood from all directions and piled it on the Paccekabuddha until
dhpak2.1:198.8: they had erected a great pyre. Then they set it alight, and saying to themselves: “Now he will burn,” they departed.
dhpak2.1:199.1: Now in the beginning their act was a thoughtless one, and they were not bound thereby. But afterwards they
dhpak2.1:199.2: committed a deliberate wrong and were bound to suffer the consequences thereof. While the Paccekabuddha was in
dhpak2.1:199.3: absorption, they might have brought a thousand cartloads of firewood and set it alight, and they could not even
dhpak2.1:199.4: have caused him to feel the heat. So on the seventh day the Paccekabuddha arose and went where he pleased.
dhpak2.1:200.1: Because they committed this wrong, those women were boiled for many hundreds of thousands of
dhpak2.1:200.2: years in Niraya Hell, and because the fruit of that same wicked deed was not yet exhausted, their
dhpak2.1:200.3: houses were burned, and they were burned in their houses in a hundred successive states of
dhpak2.1:200.4: existence in this very manner. This is the wrong they committed in a previous state of existence.
dhpak2.1:201.1: When the Teacher had related this story, the bhikkhus asked him: “But, venerable Sir,
dhpak2.1:201.2: how did Khujjuttarā come to be a hunchback? How did she become so wise? How did she obtain
dhpak2.1:201.3: the fruition of Stream-entry? How {1.226} did she become an errand-girl?” [28.292]
dhpak2.1:202.1: Bhikkhus, while that same king was ruling in Bārāṇasī, there was a Paccekabuddha who was slightly
dhpak2.1:202.2: hunchbacked. Now a certain serving-woman, throwing a blanket over her shoulder and taking a golden vessel in
dhpak2.1:202.3: her hand, bent over so that she looked like a hunchback, and saying: “This is the way our Paccekabuddha
dhpak2.1:202.4: walks,” imitated his manner of walking. It was in consequence of this that she came to be a hunchback.
dhpak2.1:203.1: But on the first day she provided those Paccekabuddhas with seats in the royal palace, took their bowls, filled
dhpak2.1:203.2: them with rice-porridge, and presented them to them. The Paccekabuddhas took the bowls of porridge, but they were
dhpak2.1:203.3: so hot that they were obliged to shift them from one hand to the other. That woman, seeing what they were doing,
dhpak2.1:203.4: presented to them eight ivory bracelets of her own, saying: “Use these bracelets as stands for your bowls.” When
dhpak2.1:203.5: they had so done, they looked at her, whereupon she said: “Venerable Sirs, we have no use for these bracelets.
dhpak2.1:203.6: Accept them as a present from us before you go.” The Paccekabuddhas took them with them to Nandamūla mountain-cave,
dhpak2.1:203.7: and those bracelets are preserved there unimpaired to this day. As the result of this act of hers, she now
dhpak2.1:203.8: knows the Three Baskets by heart and possesses profound wisdom. Likewise it was through waiting upon the Paccekabuddhas
dhpak2.1:203.9: that she obtained the fruition of Stream-entry. These were her deeds in the interval between two Buddhas.
dhpak2.1:204.1: In the dispensation of Kassapa, the Sambuddha, a certain rich man’s daughter of Bārāṇasī took her mirror one day, as
dhpak2.1:204.2: the shades of evening drew on, and sat down to adorn herself. Now a certain intimate friend of hers, {1.227} a
dhpak2.1:204.3: bhikkhunī freed from the pollutants, came to see her. For bhikkhunīs freed from the pollutants like to visit the households
dhpak2.1:204.4: of their supporters at eventide. But at that moment the rich man’s daughter happened to have no errand-girl with
dhpak2.1:204.5: her. So she said to the bhikkhunī: “I greet you, reverend lady. Just take that basket of ornaments and give it to
dhpak2.1:204.6: me.” The bhikkhunī thought to herself: “If I do not take this basket and give it to her, she will take a dislike to
dhpak2.1:204.7: me and will be reborn in Niraya Hell; but if I do give it to her, she will be reborn as the errand-girl of another.
dhpak2.1:204.8: However, it is better to be the errand-girl of another than to suffer torment in Niraya Hell.” So out of pity for her
dhpak2.1:204.9: she took the basket and gave it to her. In consequence of this act she became the errand-girl of another. [28.293]
dhpak2.1:205.1: Again one day in the Dhamma Hall the bhikkhus started a discussion. “Sāmāvatī and her five
dhpak2.1:205.2: hundred women were burned with fire in their house; as for Māgandiyā and her kinswomen, a
dhpak2.1:205.3: fire of straw was built over their bodies, and their bodies were torn asunder with iron
dhpak2.1:205.4: plows, and Māgandiyā was boiled in boiling oil. Which of these are alive and which are dead?”
dhpak2.1:206.1: The Teacher came in and asked: “Bhikkhus, what are you sitting here now talking about?” When they
dhpak2.1:206.2: told him, he said to them: “Bhikkhus, they that are heedless, though they live a hundred years, yet
dhpak2.1:206.3: are they dead. They that are heedful, be they dead or alive, yet are they alive. Māgandiyā, while
dhpak2.1:206.4: she yet lived, was dead already. Sāmāvatī and her followers, though they be dead, yet are they
dhpak2.1:206.5: alive. For, bhikkhus, the heedful never die.” So saying, he pronounced the following verses: {1.228}
dhpak2.1:207.1: Heedfulness is the deathless state, heedlessness the state of the dead,
dhpak2.1:207.2: the heedful do not die, but those who are heedless are as if dead.
dhpak2.1:208.1: The wise, fully understanding this in regard to heedfulness,
dhpak2.1:208.2: rejoice in heedfulness, delight in the domain of Noble Ones.
dhpak2.1:209.1: Those who meditate all the time constant and firm in their effort,
dhpak2.1:209.2: those wise ones will reach Nibbāna, the unsurpassed release from bonds.
dhpak2.1:215.1: At the conclusion of the teaching many became Stream-enterers
dhpak2.1:215.2: and so on, and benefit arose to many people from the teaching.
